PUBLIC RESPONSE: Thanks for the careful mapping of s.71 OSA and the NI 45-106 carve-outs, it’s helpful to keep the statutory text front and centre.

OSA s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies”, a loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation etc. Reg 1015 s.5 and the NI 45-106 restatement carry that same formulation forward. The provision is framed as securities of the institution, not “debt securities of the institution”, and it is expressly issuer-based and purchaser-blind. That is why the fact patterns keep inserting a zero-net-asset, unemployed retail offeree – the point is to test whether the exemption turns on the purchaser at all.

Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, so a non-prospectus retail distribution of its bonds in A is the textbook illustration of the carve-out in practice. The retail nature of the offering and the purchaser profile are irrelevant there, which is consistent with the issuer-based rationale.

The same rationale is what makes D the real test of the provision. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank to which the Bank Act applies. A distribution of its shares is a distribution of securities issued by a Bank Act bank. Once the issuer condition is met, s.73(1) attaches to the distribution itself; there is no accredited-investor, eligible-investor, minimum-amount, suitability or offering-memorandum condition written into the exemption, and the number of retail investors approached does not remove it.

The debt-only gloss that is often repeated in notes comes from the tradeable-debt carve-outs in NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 and from teaching shorthand. On the face of s.73(1) the exemption is “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank”. The zero net assets / unemployed purchaser facts in D are a red herring under an issuer-based exemption, just as they would be for the bank-debt example in A. The purchaser profile is meant to show purchaser-neutrality, not to defeat the exemption.

B fails on issuer grounds, JPMorgan Chase is not a Canadian Bank Act bank issuer for the Ontario exemption on the facts stated, and C fails any accredited/eligible-investor/minimum-amount/family-friends test on the $35k salary / $10k net assets facts. That leaves the bank issuer point.

On a plain statutory reading of s.73(1) the purchaser-neutral bank exemption is not limited by security type in the Act itself, and the Fairstone Bank of Canada share distribution in D is the cleanest demonstration of that issuer-based, purchaser-blind operation in Ontario as at January 2020.

1.text:
Ontario s.71 OSA requires a prospectus unless a s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 exemption is available. As at Jan 2020 the issuer based retail carve outs that are in play are the Bank Act / financial institution debt carve out and the co-operative credit association / credit union member share carve out.

Bank debt

OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 provide the classic public, purchaser neutral exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act, the Trust and Loan Companies Act or the Insurance Companies Act applies. The exemption is issuer and security based, debt only, and it is not made conditional on accreditation, minimum amount, OM or the number of purchasers.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank to which the Bank Act applies. Bonds are debt securities. A non prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds to the Ontario retail public is the textbook bank debt exemption. The retail nature of the offering is irrelevant. Compliant.

* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the authorised foreign bank branch contemplated by the bank debt exemption. No accredited investor / OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting issuer rated debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering of the US parent’s bonds. Not compliant on the facts stated.

Equity of a bank

The s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 bank / financial institution exemption is conventionally applied as a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank is not brought within s.2.19/2.34 and no investor based backstop is stated.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the securities are shares i.e. equity. On the orthodox debt only reading of the bank exemption equity is not covered and the facts give no accredited investor, eligible investor OM, $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associate or private issuer basis for a widespread retail share offering. The zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines the absence of an investor based backstop. Not compliant on the facts as stated.

Investor based

* C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300k with a spouse. Eligible investor for OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below both thresholds. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount and no OM filing is stated. No exemption is available. Non compliant.

Credit union / caisse populaire

The co-operative credit association member share exemption is the mirror image of the bank debt exemption and is issuer / membership based. On the classic teaching reading a members only membership share distribution by a caisse populaire is prospectus exempt irrespective of the member’s financial condition.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association. The facts describe the offering as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, one of whom has $0 net assets and is unemployed, with no express members only limitation pleaded and with an out of province issuer. On a strict Ontario incorporated / members only reading the exemption is not clearly engaged on the facts as pleaded.

On the facts as stated the only distribution that is unambiguously prospectus exempt in Ontario as at January 2020 is the Bank of China Canada bond distribution in A. E is the conventional credit union analogue of A on a members only reading, B, C and D are non compliant on the facts given.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the core debate is whether the Bank Act carve-out in Ontario is truly debt-limited in the statute or whether debt-only is a teaching shorthand that has been read back into s.73.

A is the textbook illustration and the reasoning for it is solid on the facts as pleaded. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds are debt, and the exemption is issuer-based and purchaser-neutral. That is why the retail nature of the offering does not defeat it, and it is the clean bank-debt example we all recognise.

The question the fact pattern is really testing is how far that issuer-based, purchaser-blind logic goes. OSA s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 and the NI 45-106 bank provisions give effect to the same carve-out. The statutory language is securities of a Bank Act bank, not debt securities of a Bank Act bank, and the exemption is expressly not qualified by the purchaser’s net assets, income or employment status.

That is why D is written the way it is. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank to which the Bank Act applies. The securities being distributed are its shares, which are securities issued by that bank. Once the issuer qualification is met the exemption attaches to the distribution itself. It does not impose an accredited investor, eligible investor, minimum amount or suitability test on offerees and it is not lost because the offering is made to a large, unselected retail base. The zero dollars net assets and unemployed offeree in the fact pattern is the classic red-herring for a purchaser-blind exemption: if the exemption were investor-based that offeree would defeat it, but the point of the bank carve-out is that the purchaser profile is irrelevant.

The debt-only reading that Colleagues 1, 10, 11, 12, 15, 18, 19 and 20 rely on is a very useful practical gloss for the retail bond market and it tracks the way NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Reg 1015 s.5 is usually taught. It is also true that in practice the retail exemption is most often seen with bank debt. It is not, however, a statutory limitation in s.73(1) itself, which speaks to securities issued or guaranteed by a bank. The debt-only gloss is policy commentary about the ordinary course of the tradeable debt provisions, not a textual bar on equity of a Bank Act bank.

B fails on issuer grounds, JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company and no Canadian Bank Act issuer, authorized foreign bank branch, accredited investor, OM or minimum amount basis is pleaded for a broad Canadian retail offering. C fails any investor-based test, salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below accredited and eligible investor thresholds and there is no family/friends/business associate or $150k minimum amount connection.

E is the credit-union analogue and it is analytically attractive, but on the facts as pleaded it is messier: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association and the offering is described as aimed at a large number of retail investors, not as a members-only membership share distribution. The provincial / member-only scope issue is exactly why E is normally used as a contrast rather than the clean illustration.

On a proper issuer-based reading of s.73, the Fairstone Bank of Canada share distribution is prospectus-exempt in Ontario as at January 2020, and the purchaser’s financial condition, including the zero net asset unemployed offeree, is immaterial to its availability. A remains the classic bank-debt example of the same issuer-based principle, but D is the direct extension of that principle to equity and it is the cleanest test of purchaser-neutrality in the list.

I think the core debate is whether the Bank Act carve-out in Ontario is truly debt-limited in the statute or whether debt-only is a teaching shorthand that has been read back into s.73.

A is the textbook illustration and the reasoning for it is solid on the facts as pleaded. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds are debt, and the exemption is issuer-based and purchaser-neutral. That is why the retail nature of the offering does not defeat it, and it is the clean bank-debt example we all recognise.

The question the fact pattern is really testing is how far that issuer-based, purchaser-blind logic goes. OSA s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 and the NI 45-106 bank provisions give effect to the same carve-out. The statutory language is securities of a Bank Act bank, not debt securities of a Bank Act bank, and the exemption is expressly not qualified by the purchaser’s net assets, income or employment status.

That is why D is written the way it is. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank to which the Bank Act applies. The securities being distributed are its shares, which are securities issued by that bank. Once the issuer qualification is met the exemption attaches to the distribution itself. It does not impose an accredited investor, eligible investor, minimum amount or suitability test on offerees and it is not lost because the offering is made to a large, unselected retail base. The zero dollars net assets and unemployed offeree in the fact pattern is the classic red-herring for a purchaser-blind exemption: if the exemption were investor-based that offeree would defeat it, but the point of the bank carve-out is that the purchaser profile is irrelevant.

The debt-only reading that Colleagues 1, 10, 11, 12, 15, 18, 19 and 20 rely on is a very useful practical gloss for the retail bond market and it tracks the way NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Reg 1015 s.5 is usually taught. It is also true that in practice the retail exemption is most often seen with bank debt. It is not, however, a statutory limitation in s.73(1) itself, which speaks to securities issued or guaranteed by a bank. The debt-only gloss is policy commentary about the ordinary course of the tradeable debt provisions, not a textual bar on equity of a Bank Act bank.

B fails on issuer grounds, JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company and no Canadian Bank Act issuer, authorized foreign bank branch, accredited investor, OM or minimum amount basis is pleaded for a broad Canadian retail offering. C fails any investor-based test, salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below accredited and eligible investor thresholds and there is no family/friends/business associate or $150k minimum amount connection.

E is the credit-union analogue and it is analytically attractive, but on the facts as pleaded it is messier: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association and the offering is described as aimed at a large number of retail investors, not as a members-only membership share distribution. The provincial / member-only scope issue is exactly why E is normally used as a contrast rather than the clean illustration.

On a proper issuer-based reading of s.73, the Fairstone Bank of Canada share distribution is prospectus-exempt in Ontario as at January 2020, and the purchaser’s financial condition, including the zero net asset unemployed offeree, is immaterial to its availability. A remains the classic bank-debt example of the same issuer-based principle, but D is the direct extension of that principle to equity and it is the cleanest test of purchaser-neutrality in the list.

Ontario s.71 OSA is displaced as at Jan 2020 by a statutory/NI 45-106 exemption. The two issuer-based retail carve-outs that are relevant here are the bank/financial institution exemption and the cooperative credit association/credit union member-share exemption. Both are issuer/membership based and purchaser neutral.

Bank / financial institution debt

OSA s.73 / O Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 exempts a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act, Trust and Loan Companies Act or Insurance Companies Act applies. The exemption is issuer and security based, debt only on the conventional teaching application, and not conditional on accreditation, minimum amount or the size of the offering.

A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II bank to which the Bank Act applies. Bonds are debt securities. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China (Canada) bonds to the Ontario retail public is the textbook bank-debt exemption. The retail nature of the offering is irrelevant. A is unambiguously prospectus exempt in Ontario as at January 2020.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is the U.S. parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian branch of an authorized foreign bank for the domestic s.2.19/2.34 exemption. No accredited investor / offering memorandum / $150k minimum amount / reporting-issuer rated debt facts are pleaded for a large public Canadian offering. B is not exempt on the facts stated.

C. Private issuer equity to an unrelated purchaser. Accredited individual NI 45-106 s.2.3 requires net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex residence or net income ≥ $200k in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300k with a spouse. Eligible investor for OM requires net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below both thresholds. There is no family/friends/business associate/employee connection and no $150k minimum amount. No exemption is available. C is non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the conventionally applied s.73/NI 45-106 bank/financial institution exemption is taught and applied as a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank is not covered by the bank-debt carve-out. No accredited investor, eligible investor OM, $150k minimum amount or private issuer relationship is stated for a widespread retail share offering and the zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines the absence of an investor-based backstop. On the orthodox debt-only reading D is not exempt. The minority statutory-text argument that OSA s.73(1) “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank” extends to equity is the source of the split in the room, but it is not the dominant exam application of the bank-debt carve-out.

Co-operative credit association

A distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association/credit union is issuer/membership based and not conditioned on purchaser financial condition. On the conventional teaching reading E would be the credit-union analogue of A. On the facts as pleaded the offering is described as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, one of whom has zero net assets and is unemployed, with no express members-only limitation pleaded and with an issuer incorporated in New Brunswick. On a strict Ontario-incorporation/member-only reading that defeats the clean application of the exemption in Ontario. E is therefore not unambiguously compliant as pleaded.

Hence the only distribution that is uncontroversially prospectus compliant in Ontario as at January 2020 on the facts given is A, the Bank of China (Canada) bond distribution under the Canadian Bank Act bank-debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the orthodox debt-only reading, and E is factually/territorially uncertain as pleaded.

The debate really comes down to how we read OSA s.73(1) and the bank / financial institution carve-out that is carried into Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106.

s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in or distribution of securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation to which the relevant federal Act applies. The statutory language is securities issued or guaranteed by the institution. It is not securities issued or guaranteed by the institution that are debt securities, and it is not conditioned on accredited investor status, minimum amount, net assets, income or the size of the retail distribution.

That issuer-based, purchaser-neutral structure is why the fact patterns keep putting in a zero net asset unemployed retail offeree. The point is not to defeat the exemption; the point is to show it does not turn on the purchaser’s financial condition. Once the issuer qualification is met the exemption attaches to the distribution itself.

Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank so its bonds in A are clearly within that issuer-based exemption and that is the textbook debt illustration. The same issuer condition is met by Fairstone Bank of Canada in D. Fairstone is a federally regulated Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. Common shares of Fairstone are securities issued by a bank to which the Bank Act applies.

On the plain text of s.73(1) the exemption is to securities of a Bank Act bank and the purchaser profile is irrelevant. The debt-only gloss that is often repeated in course notes comes from NI 45-106 s.2.34 / s.2.19 tradeable-debt commentary and from the ordinary course in which the bank carve-out is encountered. It is a teaching shorthand, not a statutory limitation. The exemption is not made conditional on debt vs equity for a Bank Act bank, and it is not lost because the offering is made to a large number of retail investors or because one offeree has $0 net assets and is unemployed. Those facts are a feature of an issuer-based exemption, not a bug.

That is the same logic that makes the co-operative credit association / caisse populaire member share exemption work in E: issuer / membership based, purchaser blind. If we accept that membership equity of a regulated co-operative can be distributed without a prospectus irrespective of the member’s net worth, the parallel issuer-based rationale for securities of a Bank Act bank should be read consistently.

B fails on issuer grounds: JPMorgan Chase & Co is the U.S. parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank issuer for the Ontario exemption and no accredited / OM / minimum amount basis is pleaded. I agree with the core of the bank-debt analysis that is being put forward for A and that is why the facts are written the way they are.

A is the textbook illustration. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19 / s.2.34 give a public, purchaser-neutral exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank to which the Bank Act applies. The retail nature of the offering and the number of purchasers is immaterial. On that basis A is prospectus-exempt in Ontario as at Jan 2020, and B fails on the foreign-parent issuer point, C fails the accredited / eligible investor / $150k minimum amount / family/friends tests on $35k salary / $10k net assets, and E is messy on provincial scope and on a members-only reading as pleaded.

The point the fact pattern is testing is whether the bank carve-out is truly issuer-based and purchaser-neutral. OSA s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust company or insurance corporation to which the relevant federal Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19 carry that forward. The statutory wording is securities issued or guaranteed by a bank, not “debt securities issued by a bank”.

The “debt only” gloss that is repeatedly cited comes from the policy discussion of tradeable debt in NI 45-106 s.2.34 and from OSC Policy 45-501, not from the wording of s.73(1) itself. The issuer condition is the Bank Act bank condition; there is no accredited investor, net asset, income, minimum amount or suitability condition written into the exemption, and that is precisely why the drafters insert a zero net asset unemployed retail purchaser into D and E – to test purchaser-neutrality.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank to which the Bank Act applies. Common shares are securities of that bank. Once the issuer qualification is met the exemption attaches to the distribution itself. It does not impose an accredited investor / eligible investor / offering memorandum / $150k minimum amount test on the offerees, and it does not turn on how large or how retail the distribution is. The zero net assets / unemployed purchaser in D is therefore a red herring under an issuer-based exemption; it is evidence the exemption is purchaser-blind, just as the retail base in A shows it is not a private placement.

That is why the issuer-based reading makes D prospectus-exempt on the facts as stated. A is the classic debt illustration of the same s.73 bank carve-out. The more complete test of the issuer-based principle, and the one that forces the security-type question, is D: a non-prospectus distribution of the shares of a Bank Act bank to a broad retail base including a non-accredited unemployed offeree. On the plain text of s.73(1) that distribution falls within the bank securities exemption in the same way Bank of China Canada bonds do.

E remains the credit-union analogue, but on the facts as pleaded it is described as a general retail distribution to a large number of retail investors, not a members-only membership share offering, and Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick caisse populaire. That provincial / member-only uncertainty is why E is not the clean illustration. B and C remain non-compliant on the stated facts.

On a proper statutory reading of the Bank Act bank exemption as issuer-based and purchaser-neutral, the distribution in D is compliant, and it demonstrates the same issuer-based logic that makes A work, just extended to equity.

Ontario s.71 OSA / NI 45-106 is an exemption based regime. As at Jan 2020 the issuer-based retail carve-outs that are in play here are the Bank Act / financial institution debt exemption and the co-operative credit association / credit union membership share exemption. The investor-based exemptions are accredited / eligible / offering memorandum / $150k minimum amount / family friends / business associate.

* Bank / financial institution debt
OSA s.73 / Ont Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19 / s.2.34 give a public, purchaser-neutral exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act, Trust and Loan Companies Act or Insurance Companies Act applies. The exemption is issuer / security based, debt only, and it is not made conditional on the number of purchasers or on purchaser financial condition.

A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail investors in Ontario is the classic bank-debt exemption. The retail nature of the offering is irrelevant. A is prospectus exempt.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the U.S. parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the authorized foreign bank branch issuer contemplated by the bank debt exemption. No accredited investor / offering memorandum / $150k minimum amount / reporting-issuer rated debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering of the U.S. parent’s bonds. B is not exempt on the facts stated.

C. Private issuer equity to an unrelated purchaser.
Accredited individual Jan 2020 NI 45-106 s.2.3: net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM: net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or pre-tax income ≥ $75k. Minimum amount $150k.
Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below both thresholds. There is no family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount and no OM filing is stated. No exemption is available. C is prospectus required.

* Bank equity
The bank / s.73 exemption as it is applied in Ontario is a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank is not brought within s.73/Reg 1015 s.5/NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares. The bank-debt exemption does not extend to equity. No accredited investor, eligible investor OM, $150k minimum amount or family/friends/business associate basis is stated for a widespread retail share offering and the zero net asset unemployed offeree merely underlines the absence of an investor-based backstop. On the orthodox debt-only teaching reading D is not exempt.

* Credit union / caisse populaire
In principle a distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / credit union is issuer / membership based and the purchaser’s financial condition is irrelevant. The zero-net-asset / unemployed offeree is the classic red herring for an issuer-based exemption.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association. The facts describe a distribution aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, one of whom has $0 net assets and is unemployed, with no express members-only limitation pleaded and with an out-of-province issuer. On a strict Ontario-incorporated / members-only reading the cooperative exemption is not clearly engaged on the facts as stated, and the offering is pleaded as a general public retail offering rather than a members-only membership share distribution. That is the residual provincial/membership problem that prevents E from being unambiguously compliant as pleaded.

On the facts as stated the only uncontested, textbook compliant transaction is the classic bank-debt distribution in A. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts given, and E is not unambiguously compliant as pleaded on the provincial/members-only reading. If the credit-union member-only condition were assumed to be met, E is the conventional credit-union analogue of A.

I think the issuer-based nature of the bank exemption is being under-read by the debt-only gloss that is being repeated for A.

OSA s.71 requires a prospectus unless an exemption is available. OSA s.73(1) and O Reg 1015 s.5, carried forward in NI 45-106 s.2.19, displace the prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the relevant federal Act applies. The statutory formulation is securities of the institution, not “debt securities of the institution”, and the exemption is deliberately purchaser-neutral. It is not made conditional on accredited-investor status, eligible-investor financial thresholds, minimum amount, offering memorandum, or the number or sophistication of the purchasers.

That purchaser-neutrality is precisely what the fact pattern is testing. D describes a non-prospectus distribution of shares by Fairstone Bank of Canada to a large retail base, one offeree having zero dollars net assets and being unemployed. If the exemption were investor-based the profile would defeat it. The profile is included to show the exemption does not turn on the purchaser at all.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. Its common shares are securities issued by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. On the plain text of s.73(1) the exemption attaches to securities issued by a Bank Act bank and is not limited by security type in the Act. The debt-only reading is a teaching shorthand that conflates the core s.73 issuer exemption with the tradeable-debt restatement in NI 45-106 s.2.34 / s.2.35. The policy rationale for the carve-out is the same as for the co-operative credit association member-share exemption discussed for E: regulation of the issuer substitutes for purchaser qualification.

Bank of China (Canada) bonds in A are also within the same issuer-based carve-out, which is why A is the classic debt illustration. The point of D is that the exemption is not confined to debt securities of a Bank Act bank. Once the issuer condition is met the exemption is available for the bank’s securities generally, and the zero-net-asset unemployed retail offeree is immaterial.

B is not made out on issuer grounds. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not debt of a Canadian Bank Act bank or an authorized foreign bank branch operating in Canada, and no accredited-investor / offering-memorandum / $150k minimum amount basis is pleaded for a broad Canadian retail offering.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020 is exemption based under OSA s.71, s.73 / Reg 1015 and NI 45-106. Issuer-based retail carve-outs are central: Bank Act financial institution debt/securities and co-operative credit association/credit union member share. Investor-based backstops are accredited investor, eligible investor for OM, minimum amount $150k, family/friends/business associate.

Bank debt
* Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. Non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to retail investors is the classic issuer-based purchaser-neutral bank-debt exemption under NI 45-106 s.2.19/s.2.34 / OSA s.73/Reg 1015 s.5. No accredited/eligible/minimum test applies. Unanimously held compliant. A is unambiguously compliant.

* JPMorgan Chase & Co is US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank / authorized foreign bank branch on facts. No accredited/OM/minimum amount/reporting-issuer rated debt reliance pleaded for a large public Canadian offering. Universally held non-compliant. B is non-compliant.

Private issuer / accredited
* C shares of private issuer to unrelated individual; salary $35k, net assets $10k. Accredited individual Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excl principal residence OR net income ≥ $200k in each last two years and reasonable expectation current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM: net assets ≥ $400k excl residence OR pre-tax income ≥ $75k. Minimum amount $150k. Purchaser below all thresholds, no family/friends/business associate/employee connection, no OM filing. Universally non-compliant. C is non-compliant.

Bank equity – core dispute
* D Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to large retail base, one offeree zero net assets unemployed.
Majority/orthodox teaching: s.73/NI 45-106 s.2.19 bank exemption is debt securities only. Equity of a bank is not covered; would need accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/private issuer basis, absent. Zero-asset unemployed offeree underlines lack of investor backstop → non-compliant.
Minority/plain-text: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus for trades in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which Bank Act applies. Statutory text says securities, not debt securities, issuer-based and purchaser-neutral. Fairstone Bank of Canada is Schedule III Bank Act bank; its shares are securities of that bank; purchaser financial condition irrelevant. On this reading D is exempt and is the clean equity test of purchaser neutrality.

Credit union / caisse populaire – second dispute
* E Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to large retail investors, one offeree zero net assets unemployed.
Conventional teaching: co-operative credit association member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser-neutral; member financial condition irrelevant. On textbook reading E is mirror of A and would be exempt irrespective of offeree net assets/employment.
Caveats repeatedly raised: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is New Brunswick caisse; facts describe general retail offering not expressly members-only; strict Ontario reading may limit exemption to Ontario credit unions and to members-only offerings. Hence a split: many treat E as compliant credit-union analogue of A; others find it not unambiguously compliant due to provincial scope and lack of members-only limitation pleaded.

Current best synthesis
A is the only uncontroversially compliant distribution on facts as stated. B and C are clearly non-compliant. D remains the main point of dissent: orthodox debt-only reading = non-compliant; plain-text issuer-based securities reading = compliant. E is the conventional credit-union analogue and commonly taught as compliant if members-only condition is assumed; as pleaded it is factually messy on membership/provincial scope, so only A is unambiguous without further factual assumptions.

Unresolved questions retained
* Does OSA s.73(1) limit bank exemption to debt or to securities generally? Debt-only practice vs statutory wording securities issued/guaranteed by a bank.
* Credit union exemption territorial/membership scope: does New Brunswick caisse populaire’s shares to Ontario retail investors fall within Ontario exemption, and must offering be explicitly members-only?
* Whether JPMorgan Chase debt could be caught by authorized foreign bank / tradeable debt NI 45-106 s.2.24/2.35 – not pleaded on facts.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian branch of an authorized foreign bank issuer contemplated by s.2.19/2.34. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/reporting issuer rated debt facts pleaded for a large public Canadian offering. Majority non-compliant. Minority dissent argues bank-debt exemption is broad to chartered banks and marketing does not defeat it.

C. Private issuer shares to unrelated individual. Salary $35k, net assets $10k. No family/friends/business associate connection. Not accredited: <$200k income and <$1M net assets. Not eligible for OM: <$75k income and <$400k net assets. No $150k minimum amount stated. Consensus non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank. Securities are shares i.e. equity. Majority/dominant debt-only reading: s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 s.2.19 bank exemption is debt securities only. Equity of a bank is not covered. No accredited/eligible/minimum amount basis shown; zero net asset unemployed purchaser underlines absence of investor based backstop. Therefore non-compliant.

Minority plain-text reading: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 carry the same formulation. Statutory wording is securities of the bank, not debt securities of the bank, and the exemption is issuer-based and purchaser-neutral by design. Fairstone is a Bank Act bank, common shares are securities issued by that bank, and the purchaser profile is a red herring. Under that reading D is compliant and actually tests purchaser neutrality more cleanly than A. This is the main split in the room.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a provincial co-operative credit association/caisse populaire. The credit union/co-operative member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser blind; member financial condition is irrelevant. Majority view: on a members-only reading the distribution of membership shares by a caisse populaire/credit union is prospectus exempt irrespective of members’ financial condition, making E the credit-union analogue of A.

Residual uncertainty: facts describe offering “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors”, not expressly members-only, and issuer is New Brunswick, raising provincial scope/member-only limitation questions. Some colleagues treat E as compliant on conventional teaching; others treat it as not clearly engaged as pleaded. If the member-only condition is assumed, E is the second issuer-based illustration.

Current synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant. C is unambiguously non-compliant. B is non-compliant on dominant reading. D is non-compliant on dominant debt-only reading but a substantial minority argues D is compliant under a literal s.73 securities reading and would be the cleanest issuer-based test. E is plausibly compliant under the credit-union/member exemption with factual/provincial caveats. The most defensible single textbook answer remains A, Bank of China Canada bonds under the Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption; D is the live statutory interpretation split, E is the credit-union analogue if membership condition accepted.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares/equity. The zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines lack of investor-based backstop. D non-compliant on orthodox teaching.

Once issuer qualification is met there is no accredited/eligible/minimum amount/suitability condition, and number of retail investors is immaterial. reflection_text.6:
Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020 is exemption based under OSA s.71, s.73 / Reg 1015 and NI 45-106. Issuer-based retail carve-outs are central: Bank Act financial institution debt/securities and co-operative credit association/credit union member share. Investor-based backstops are accredited investor, eligible investor for OM, minimum amount $150k, family/friends/business associate.

Bank debt
* Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. Non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to retail investors is the classic issuer-based purchaser-neutral bank-debt exemption under NI 45-106 s.2.19/s.2.34 / OSA s.73/Reg 1015 s.5. No accredited/eligible/minimum test applies. Unanimously held compliant. A is unambiguously compliant.

* JPMorgan Chase & Co is US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank / authorized foreign bank branch on facts. No accredited/OM/minimum amount/reporting-issuer rated debt reliance pleaded for a large public Canadian offering. Universally held non-compliant. B is non-compliant.

Private issuer / accredited
* C shares of private issuer to unrelated individual; salary $35k, net assets $10k. Accredited individual Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excl principal residence OR net income ≥ $200k in each last two years and reasonable expectation current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM: net assets ≥ $400k excl residence OR pre-tax income ≥ $75k. Minimum amount $150k. Purchaser below all thresholds, no family/friends/business associate/employee connection, no OM filing. Universally non-compliant. C is non-compliant.

Bank equity – core dispute
* D Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to large retail base, one offeree zero net assets unemployed.
Majority/orthodox teaching: s.73/NI 45-106 s.2.19 bank exemption is debt securities only. Equity of a bank is not covered; would need accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/private issuer basis, absent. Zero-asset unemployed offeree underlines lack of investor backstop → non-compliant.
Minority/plain-text: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus for trades in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which Bank Act applies. Statutory text says securities, not debt securities, issuer-based and purchaser-neutral. Fairstone Bank of Canada is Schedule III Bank Act bank; its shares are securities of that bank; purchaser financial condition irrelevant. On this reading D is exempt and is the clean equity test of purchaser neutrality.

Credit union / caisse populaire – second dispute
* E Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to large retail investors, one offeree zero net assets unemployed.
Conventional teaching: co-operative credit association member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser-neutral; member financial condition irrelevant. On textbook reading E is mirror of A and would be exempt irrespective of offeree net assets/employment.
Caveats repeatedly raised: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is New Brunswick caisse; facts describe general retail offering not expressly members-only; strict Ontario reading may limit exemption to Ontario credit unions and to members-only offerings. Hence a split: many treat E as compliant credit-union analogue of A; others find it not unambiguously compliant due to provincial scope and lack of members-only limitation pleaded.

Current best synthesis
A is the only uncontroversially compliant distribution on facts as stated. B and C are clearly non-compliant. D remains the main point of dissent: orthodox debt-only reading = non-compliant; plain-text issuer-based securities reading = compliant. E is the conventional credit-union analogue and commonly taught as compliant if members-only condition is assumed; as pleaded it is factually messy on membership/provincial scope, so only A is unambiguous without further factual assumptions.

Unresolved questions retained
* Does OSA s.73(1) limit bank exemption to debt or to securities generally? Debt-only practice vs statutory wording securities issued/guaranteed by a bank.
* Credit union exemption territorial/membership scope: does New Brunswick caisse populaire’s shares to Ontario retail investors fall within Ontario exemption, and must offering be explicitly members-only?
* Whether JPMorgan Chase debt could be caught by authorized foreign bank / tradeable debt NI 45-106 s.2.24/2.35 – not pleaded on facts.
reflection_text.12:
Legal framework as of Jan 2020 Ontario: prospectus required unless OSA s.73 / NI 45-106 statutory exemption applies. Key issuer-based exemptions: bank/debt securities exemption; cooperative credit union/caisse populaire member securities exemption; investor-based: accredited investor, offering memorandum/eligible investor, minimum $150k, family/friends/business associates.

Bank debt exemption
* NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 / OSA s.73 / Ont Reg 1015 s.5. Practically taught as debt securities of Bank Act bank, loan corporation, trust company, insurance company. Exemption is issuer/security based, purchaser-neutral.
* Bank of China (Canada) = Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds = debt. Distribution to retail public without prospectus = textbook compliant. Consensus across rounds, unambiguously compliant. A is clear.
* JPMorgan Chase = U.S. parent. Majority view: bank-debt exemption does not extend to foreign parent debt on facts given; no accredited/OM/minimum amount stated. Minority Colleague 13/18 argue foreign bank debt is covered via authorized foreign bank/tradeable debt. Current weight favors non-compliant.
* Fairstone Bank of Canada = Schedule III Bank Act bank. Core disagreement persists on security type.
  - Majority 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8 argue bank exemption is debt-only; equity shares not covered, D non-compliant.
  - Minority 13,14,16,17,21,5,7,9,2 argue OSA s.73(1) wording “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank” is issuer-based and not limited to debt, so D would be compliant and purchaser profile irrelevant.
  Debt-only is orthodox exam reading; statutory text dispute remains unresolved.

Accredited/eligible investor thresholds
* Accredited individual: net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence, or net income ≥ $200k each of last 2 years and reasonable expectation current year, $300k with spouse; or $5m net assets.
* Eligible investor for OM: net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or pre-tax income ≥ $75k.
* Minimum amount: $150,000 purchase price.

C = private issuer shares to unrelated individual with salary $35k, net assets $10k. Well below accredited and eligible thresholds. No family/friends connection, no minimum amount stated. Consensus non-compliant.

Credit union/caisse populaire
* NI 45-106 / OSA s.73 cooperative credit association exemption for distribution of membership securities by a credit union/caisse populaire to members. Exemption is issuer/membership based, purchaser financial condition irrelevant.
* E = Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to large retail group, one offeree zero net assets unemployed. Majority teaching view: exemption available if member-only; financial condition irrelevant. Dispute on facts: offering described as aimed at “a large number of retail investors” not expressly members-only, and issuer is New Brunswick. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,20,3 argue provincial scope/member-only defeats clean application; colleagues 2,4,6,8,18,19 argue classic credit-union illustration and would be compliant. E remains plausible but not unambiguously compliant on facts as pleaded.

Current belief after round 2
* A is unambiguously compliant.
* B and C are non-compliant on facts as stated.
* D is non-compliant on orthodox debt-only reading of bank exemption; minority statutory-text reading would make D compliant. Debt-only reading remains dominant in deliberation.
* E is plausibly compliant under credit-union member exemption, though facts about non-member retail public and extraprovincial caisse populaire create uncertainty. If a single best uncontroversial answer is required, A alone is clear.

Unresolved questions for next round
* Does OSA s.73 bank exemption as interpreted in practice cover equity securities of a Bank Act bank or is it limited to debt? Securities wording vs NI 45-106 s.2.19 debt carve-out.
* Does credit union exemption apply to New Brunswick caisse populaire offering to Ontario retail investors, and does fact pattern require member-only language to be satisfied?
* Is JPMorgan Chase debt covered by authorized foreign bank/tradeable debt exemption NI 45-106 s.2.24/2.35 on these facts?

Information retained from earlier rounds that remains important: Bank of China (Canada) Schedule II status, Fairstone Bank Schedule III status, accredited/eligible thresholds, minimum amount $150k, member-based nature of credit union exemption, purchaser-neutrality of issuer-based exemptions.
reflection_text.4:
The Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020 is exemption based. Core issuer-based retail carve outs are the Bank Act financial institution debt carve out and the co-operative credit association/credit union member share carve out. Investor based backstops are accredited investor NI 45-106 s.2.3 – net assets ≥ $1M ex residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonable expectation current year; eligible investor for OM – net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k; minimum amount investment $150k.

Bank / financial institution debt
OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is the classic purchaser-neutral retail exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act etc applies. Conventional teaching and most colleagues apply it as debt only, issuer/security based, not conditioned on accreditation, number of purchasers or suitability.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. Non-prospectus distribution to Ontario retail investors is the textbook bank-debt exemption. Unanimous. Compliant.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian branch of an authorized foreign bank issuer contemplated by s.2.19/2.34. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/reporting issuer rated debt facts pleaded for a large public Canadian offering. Majority non-compliant. Minority dissent argues bank-debt exemption is broad to chartered banks and marketing does not defeat it.

C. Private issuer shares to unrelated individual. Salary $35k, net assets $10k. No family/friends/business associate connection. Not accredited: <$200k income and <$1M net assets. Not eligible for OM: <$75k income and <$400k net assets. No $150k minimum amount stated. Consensus non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank. Securities are shares i.e. equity. Majority/dominant debt-only reading: s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 s.2.19 bank exemption is debt securities only. Equity of a bank is not covered. No accredited/eligible/minimum amount basis shown; zero net asset unemployed purchaser underlines absence of investor based backstop. Therefore non-compliant.

Minority plain-text reading: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 carry the same formulation. Statutory wording is securities of the bank, not debt securities of the bank, and the exemption is issuer-based and purchaser-neutral by design. Fairstone is a Bank Act bank, common shares are securities issued by that bank, and the purchaser profile is a red herring. Under that reading D is compliant and actually tests purchaser neutrality more cleanly than A. This is the main split in the room.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a provincial co-operative credit association/caisse populaire. The credit union/co-operative member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser blind; member financial condition is irrelevant. Majority view: on a members-only reading the distribution of membership shares by a caisse populaire/credit union is prospectus exempt irrespective of members’ financial condition, making E the credit-union analogue of A.

Residual uncertainty: facts describe offering “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors”, not expressly members-only, and issuer is New Brunswick, raising provincial scope/member-only limitation questions. Some colleagues treat E as compliant on conventional teaching; others treat it as not clearly engaged as pleaded. If the member-only condition is assumed, E is the second issuer-based illustration.

Current synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant. C is unambiguously non-compliant. B is non-compliant on dominant reading. D is non-compliant on dominant debt-only reading but a substantial minority argues D is compliant under a literal s.73 securities reading and would be the cleanest issuer-based test. E is plausibly compliant under the credit-union/member exemption with factual/provincial caveats. The most defensible single textbook answer remains A, Bank of China Canada bonds under the Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption; D is the live statutory interpretation split, E is the credit-union analogue if membership condition accepted.
reflection_text.10:
The deliberation remains anchored on the issuer-based retail carve-outs in Ontario as at Jan 2020: the Bank Act / financial institution debt exemption in OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 and the co-operative credit association / credit union member-share exemption. Investor-based backstops are accredited investor NI 45-106 s.2.3, eligible investor for OM, $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associate.

A is the uncontroversial textbook case. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. The exemption is issuer/security based, purchaser neutral, not conditioned on number of purchasers or financial condition. A non-prospectus retail bond distribution is clearly exempt. All colleagues agree A is compliant.

B is non-compliant on the stated facts. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank nor the Canadian branch of an authorized foreign bank issuer for s.2.19/2.34. No accredited investor / OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting-issuer rated debt facts are pleaded for a large public Canadian offering. The minority tradeable-debt reading exists but is not the consensus.

C is non-compliant. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. Individual accredited = net assets ≥ $1M ex residence or net income ≥ $200k in each of last two years and reasonable expectation current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35k and net assets $10k are far below. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount, no OM filing. No exemption.

D is the central split.

Majority / debt-only view: s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is conventionally applied as a debt securities exemption. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares/equity. Equity of a bank is not covered by the bank-debt carve-out, and no accredited/eligible/$150k/family-friends backstop is stated. The zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines lack of investor-based backstop. D non-compliant on orthodox teaching.

Minority / statutory-text view: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus for a trade in “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies”. Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 carry the same formulation. The statutory language is “securities”, not “debt securities”, and the exemption is issuer-based and purchaser-neutral by design. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank; its shares are securities issued by a Bank Act bank. Once issuer qualification is met there is no accredited/eligible/minimum amount/suitability condition, and number of retail investors is immaterial. The zero net asset unemployed offeree is a red herring intended to show purchaser neutrality. On plain text D is exempt. The debt-only gloss is teaching shorthand from tradeable-debt provisions.

E is the credit-union analogue. In principle a distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association/credit union is issuer/membership based and not conditioned on purchaser financial condition. The zero net asset/unemployed member is irrelevant to a members-only offering. The fact pattern is messy: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick caisse populaire, the offering is described as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors with no express members-only limitation pleaded. On a strict Ontario-incorporated / members-only reading the exemption is not clearly engaged. Majority teaching treats E as the credit-union mirror of A, compliant on a members-only reading; strict territorial/membership reading makes it not unambiguously compliant as pleaded.

Current belief: A is the clear, uncontroversial compliant distribution. B and C are non-compliant. D is contested between debt-only non-compliant majority and securities-generally compliant minority; the issue is whether OSA s.73(1) is limited to debt by statute or by convention. E is the conventional second issuer-based illustration, compliant under the credit-union member-share exemption if read as members-only, but factually qualified by provincial scope and lack of express members-only limitation. Unresolved is whether the exam expects only A, or A+E, and whether D is intended as an equity extension of the same s.73 issuer exemption.

Eligible investor for OM requires net assets ≥ $400k or income ≥ $75k. No family/friends/business associate, employee, $150k minimum amount connection. Unanimous non-compliant.

Minority view 13,14,16,17,2,5,7,9,21: OSA s.73(1) exempts “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies”. Majority: foreign parent, not a Canadian Bank Act bank, bank-debt exemption not available; no accredited/OM/minimum amount stated → non-compliant.   Debt-only majority 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8: s.73/Reg1015/NI45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is a debt securities exemption; equity of a bank is not covered; no investor-based backstop. Non-compliant.

  Majority teaching view: co-operative credit association / credit-union member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser neutral; analogue of bank exemption; E would be compliant on member-only reading.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m with the group on A being the textbook illustration we all recognise. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds are debt securities, OSA s.71 is displaced by s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 / s.2.34 and the retail nature of the offering, the number of purchasers and the purchasers’ financial condition are irrelevant. That’s uncontroversial.

Where I’m struggling is the debt-only read we keep giving to the same exemption for D. OSA s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19 carry the same formulation. The statutory text is securities issued or guaranteed by a Bank Act bank, not debt securities issued by a Bank Act bank, and the provision is framed issuer-based and purchaser-neutral with no accredited investor, eligible investor, minimum amount, OM or suitability condition written in.

That purchaser-neutrality is exactly why the fact pattern flags a large retail base and an offeree with zero net assets who is unemployed in D and in E. If the exemption were investor-based that profile would defeat it. The profile is meant to demonstrate purchaser-blindness, not to show the absence of a backstop.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. A common share of Fairstone is a security issued by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Once the issuer qualification is met the exemption attaches to the distribution. There is nothing in s.73(1) that conditions availability on the security being debt, and the number of retail investors approached does not remove it.

The “debt only” gloss that is often repeated in notes comes from the tradeable-debt commentary around NI 45-106 s.2.34 / s.2.35 and from the practical fact that the carve-out is most often seen with bank debt. That is useful shorthand, but it isn’t a textual limitation in s.73(1). On a plain reading the same issuer-based logic that makes Bank of China Canada bonds exempt makes Fairstone Bank of Canada shares exempt, and D actually tests the point more cleanly because it forces the security-type question and shows the purchaser profile is immaterial by design.

B fails on issuer grounds and C fails every investor-based test on $35k salary / $10k net assets. E is the credit union analogue but is messier on the facts as pleaded, New Brunswick issuer described as a general retail offering with no express members-only limitation.

Given the statutory wording of s.73(1) and the purchaser-neutral, issuer-based structure of the carve-out, D is the direct extension of the same s.73 bank securities exemption that underlies A, and the zero-net-asset unemployed offeree is evidence of purchaser neutrality, not a defect.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the consensus that A is the textbook illustration and uncontroversial on these facts. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds are debt securities, and OSA s.71 is displaced by the issuer-based retail carve-out in OSA s.73(1) / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 / s.2.34. The retail nature of the offering and the number of purchasers are irrelevant for that carve-out, which is why B fails on foreign issuer grounds and C fails every investor-based accredited / eligible / OM / $150k minimum / family-friends test on $35k salary / $10k net assets.

Where I think we need to be careful is the debt-only gloss that is being read back into s.73. OSA s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation to which the relevant federal Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19 give effect to the same formulation. The statutory language is securities issued or guaranteed by a bank, not debt securities issued by a bank, and the exemption is expressly issuer-based and purchaser-neutral.

That purchaser-neutrality is exactly why the fact pattern flags a large retail base and an offeree with zero net assets who is unemployed in D and E. Under an investor-based exemption that profile would defeat the exemption. Under an issuer-based exemption the profile is a feature, not a bug.

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. A common share of Fairstone is a security issued by a Bank Act bank. Once the issuer condition is met s.73 attaches to the distribution itself. There is no accredited investor, eligible investor, minimum amount, suitability or number-of-purchasers condition written into s.73, and the exemption does not, on the face of the statute, turn on debt versus equity.

The debt-only reading that is repeatedly cited is a teaching shorthand that tracks NI 45-106 s.2.34 tradeable debt commentary and OSC policy around reporting-issuer rated debt, not a textual limitation in s.73(1). That is why colleagues 10, 14 and 16 can acknowledge the plain-text securities wording while still landing on A; the minority plain-text point is real and it is the statutory basis for the same issuer-based logic that makes A work.

On that plain reading D is the direct extension of the s.73 bank securities exemption to equity and it actually tests the principle more cleanly than A, because it forces the security-type question and the purchaser-neutrality question at the same time. The zero net asset / unemployed offeree in D is the textbook demonstration of purchaser blindness, just as the broad retail base in A demonstrates it for debt.

E is the credit-union analogue and it remains messier on the facts as pleaded: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association and the offering is described as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, not as an express members-only membership share distribution. That provincial / membership scope issue is why D is the cleaner Bank Act issuer test.

On a proper statutory reading of s.73(1) as securities issued or guaranteed by a Bank Act bank, purchaser-neutral and not limited by security type in the Act itself, the Fairstone Bank of Canada share distribution without a prospectus to a broad retail base, including a non-accredited unemployed purchaser, falls within the bank securities exemption in the same way Bank of China Canada bonds do.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE:

As at Jan 2020 Ontario s.71 OSA requires a prospectus unless a s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 exemption is engaged on the facts as pleaded.

The issuer based retail carve outs that are in play here are the Bank Act / financial institution carve out and the co-operative credit association / credit union member share carve out. Both are issuer / membership based and purchaser neutral. The investor based backstops are accredited / eligible investor, OM, $150k minimum amount and family/friends/business associate/private issuer.

Bank / financial institution debt

NI 45-106 s.2.19 / s.2.34, OSA s.73 and Reg 1015 s.5 give the classic public, purchaser neutral exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act, Trust and Loan Companies Act or Insurance Companies Act applies. The exemption is issuer and security based, on the orthodox teaching application it is debt only, and it is not conditioned on accreditation, minimum amount or the number of purchasers.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds to the Ontario retail public is the textbook bank-debt exemption. The retail nature of the offering is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario as at January 2020.

* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian authorized foreign bank branch issuer contemplated by s.2.19/2.34. No accredited investor / OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting issuer rated debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering. B is not exempt on the facts stated.

Bank equity

The s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 bank / financial institution exemption that is applied in Ontario in practice is a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank is not brought within the bank debt carve out and no accredited investor, eligible investor OM, $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associate or private issuer basis is stated for a widespread retail share offering.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank, but the securities are shares i.e. equity. On the debt only reading that is the conventionally applied construction, equity is not covered. The zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines the absence of an investor based backstop. D is not exempt on the facts as stated. The minority plain-text argument for s.73(1) “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank” is noted, but that is not the debt-only construction on which the bank-debt carve-out is taught and applied in Ontario.

Investor based

* C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300k with a spouse. Eligible investor for OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below both thresholds. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount and no OM filing is stated. No exemption is available. C is non-compliant.

Co-operative credit association

A distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / credit union is issuer / membership based and not purchaser conditioned. On the conventional teaching a members only membership share distribution is prospectus exempt irrespective of the member’s financial condition.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association. The facts describe the offering as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, one of whom has $0 net assets and is unemployed, with no express members only limitation pleaded and with an extra provincial issuer. On a strict Ontario / members only reading the exemption is not clearly engaged on the facts as pleaded. It is the credit union analogue of A on a members only reading, but it is not unambiguously compliant as stated.

On the facts as pleaded the only unambiguously prospectus compliant distribution in Ontario as at January 2020 is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution under the Canadian Bank Act bank-debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the facts given on the orthodox debt-only reading of the bank exemption, and E is not unambiguously compliant as pleaded.

Ontario s.71 OSA requires a prospectus unless a s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 exemption is engaged on the facts as pleaded as at Jan 2020. Eligible investor for OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below both thresholds. On the facts as stated the only distribution that is unambiguously, non-controversially prospectus exempt in Ontario as at January 2020 is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution under the Bank Act bank debt exemption. PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the consensus that A is the textbook illustration and is compliant on the facts as stated.

Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds are debt securities, and OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 / s.2.34 give the classic public, purchaser-neutral carve-out for debt securities of a Bank Act bank. The retail nature of the offering and the number of purchasers is immaterial to that exemption, which is why B fails on issuer grounds, JPMorgan Chase & Co is the U.S. parent holding company and not a Canadian Bank Act issuer for the domestic carve-out, and C fails every investor-based test on a $35k salary / $10k net assets facts with no accredited / eligible / $150k minimum amount / family-friends connection.

Where I think we are over-reading the teaching gloss is on D. The carve-out is being described as “debt only” because that is how the bank exemption is most often encountered in practice and because NI 45-106 s.2.34 / s.2.19 tradeable-debt commentary is often conflated with the core s.73 exemption. The statutory text is different.

OSA s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in or distribution of securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation to which the relevant federal Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 give effect to the same formulation. Ontario s.71 OSA requires a prospectus unless a statutory / NI 45-106 exemption is engaged on the facts as pleaded as at January 2020.

Issuer based retail carve outs

OSA s.73(1) / O Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 are framed as issuer / security based and purchaser neutral. The statutory formulation in s.73(1) is a trade in or distribution of securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation to which the relevant federal Act applies. The exemption is deliberately not made conditional on accreditation, eligible investor status, minimum amount, offering memorandum, suitability or the number or profile of the purchasers. That purchaser neutrality is why the fact patterns repeatedly insert a zero net asset / unemployed retail offeree.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus retail distribution of the bank’s bonds into Ontario is the textbook s.73 / bank debt carve out. The retail nature of the offering is immaterial. A is unambiguously prospectus exempt.

* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian authorized foreign bank branch issuer contemplated by the bank carve out. No accredited investor / eligible investor OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting issuer rated / tradeable debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering of the US parent’s bonds. B is not exempt on the facts stated.

Investor based

* C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300k with a spouse. Eligible investor for an OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below both thresholds. There is no family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount investment and no OM filing is stated. No exemption is available. C is prospectus required.

Bank equity – issuer neutrality

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. A common share of Fairstone is a security issued by a bank to which the Bank Act applies.

On the plain text of OSA s.73(1) the exemption attaches to securities issued or guaranteed by a Bank Act bank. Once the issuer condition is met the exemption is available to the distribution itself; there is no accredited investor, eligible investor, minimum amount, suitability or number-of-purchasers condition written into s.73. The zero net assets / unemployed offeree in D is therefore the classic red herring for an issuer based, purchaser blind exemption. The same issuer based logic that makes the Bank of China Canada bond distribution in A exempt makes the Fairstone Bank of Canada share distribution in D exempt, and D is in fact the cleaner test of purchaser neutrality because it forces the security type question into equity and into a non-accredited unemployed purchaser.

The co-operative credit association / caisse populaire member share exemption is the membership analogue of the bank carve out and is likewise issuer / membership based and purchaser blind. B and C are non-compliant on the facts stated. A is the uncontroversial textbook bank securities exemption. On a proper statutory reading of OSA s.73(1) as securities of a Bank Act bank, purchaser neutral, the distribution in D is prospectus exempt in Ontario as at January 2020 and demonstrates the same issuer based rationale that underlies A.

NI 45-106 s.2.19 / s.2.34, OSA s.73 and Reg 1015 s.5 give the classic public, purchaser neutral exemption for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act, Trust and Loan Companies Act or Insurance Companies Act applies. The exemption is issuer and security based, on the orthodox teaching application it is debt only, and it is not conditioned on accreditation, minimum amount or the number of purchasers.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds to the Ontario retail public is the textbook bank-debt exemption. The retail nature of the offering is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario as at January 2020.

* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co. is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian authorized foreign bank branch issuer contemplated by s.2.19/2.34. No accredited investor / OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting issuer rated debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering. B is not exempt on the facts stated.

Bank equity

The s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 bank / financial institution exemption that is applied in Ontario in practice is a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank is not brought within the bank debt carve out and no accredited investor, eligible investor OM, $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associate or private issuer basis is stated for a widespread retail share offering.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank, but the securities are shares i.e. equity. Investor based

* C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. A distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association / credit union is issuer / membership based and not purchaser conditioned. On the conventional teaching a members only membership share distribution is prospectus exempt irrespective of the member’s financial condition.
